([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] clause (a)). The component
functions are constant, hence $C^\infty$, so $g$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field; at every $p$ the form $g_p$ is nondegenerate with
inertia $(3,1,0)$. By [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a) the
pair $(M,g)$ is therefore a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$.

**(b) The inertial chart and frame.** The chart $x$ is called the **inertial
chart** of the flat model. In this chart the coordinate frame
$(\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)$ is a $g$-orthonormal frame at
every point, $g(\partial_a,\partial_b)=\eta_{ab}$; it is simultaneously a
coordinate frame and a **tetrad field** in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]], defined on all of $M$.

**(c) Time orientation and causal classification.** Define the smooth vector
field $N:=\partial_0$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). Since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)=\eta_{00}=-1<0$ for every $p$, the field $N$ is everywhere
timelike, so $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)). For a nonzero tangent
vector $v=v^a\partial_a|_p$ the definitions of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c) and
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] give

$$g_p(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2,\qquad g_p(v,N_p)=-v^0 .$$

so $v$ is **future-directed** exactly when $v^0>0$, and

- $v$ is future timelike $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2>\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is future null $\iff$ $v^0>0$ and $(v^0)^2=\sum_i(v^i)^2$;
- $v$ is spacelike $\iff$ $(v^0)^2<\sum_i(v^i)^2$;

consequently the future causal cone at every point is
$\{v\neq0: v^0\ge\sqrt{\sum_i(v^i)^2}\}$. These are the standard readings of
the Minkowski form in the inertial chart; the chain of equivalences is the
specialization of the causal classification to this pair $(g_p,N_p)$ and is
recorded here for later use.

**(d) Scope.** This item defines geometric data only: a manifold, a metric
field, a time orientation and a distinguished chart and frame. It makes no
claim about curvature, about any field equation, about which geometry a
physical model uses, or about nature; the physical reading of the data, the
dimensions of the coordinates and the numerical values or signs of physical
constants belong to the framework's unit conventions and postulates, which
are separate items. In particular no relation between the coordinate
functions $x^a$ and physical time or length measurements is asserted here.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart ([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]), let $(n,s)$
be an observer and propagation direction and let $p$, $h$, $\Sigma(n,s)$,
$\Pi_{n,s}$ and the amplitude terminology be as in
[[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]]. Write $V:=\mathbb R^4$ and let
$\mathcal S$ be the space of symmetric covariant $2$-tensors on $V$. Then:

**(a) Projections.** $p$ and $h$ are linear endomorphisms of $V$ with
$p^2=p$, $h^2=h$, $\ker p=\operatorname{span}\{n,s\}$,
$\operatorname{im}p=\Sigma(n,s)$, $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$,
$\operatorname{im}h=n^\perp$; both are $\eta$-self-adjoint,
$\eta(pu,v)=\eta(u,pv)$ and $\eta(hu,v)=\eta(u,hv)$ for all $u,v$. Moreover
$h-p=s^\flat\otimes s$, that is $h^a{}_b-p^a{}_b=s^as_b$.

**(b) Ranks and traces.** $\operatorname{rank}p=\dim\Sigma(n,s)=2$,
$p^a{}_a=2$, $\operatorname{rank}h=3$, $h^a{}_a=3$.

**(c) TT projection.** $\Pi_{n,s}$ is a linear endomorphism of $\mathcal S$
with $\Pi_{n,s}^2=\Pi_{n,s}$; for every $A\in\mathcal S$ the tensor
$\Pi_{n,s}(A)$ is TT with respect to $(n,s)$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]] clause (d); and $\Pi_{n,s}(A)=A$
exactly when $A$ is TT. The TT tensors form the two-dimensional linear
subspace $T_{n,s}=\{B\in\mathcal S:B(n,\cdot)=B(s,\cdot)=0,\ \eta^{ab}B_{ab}=0\}$,
so $\dim T_{n,s}=2$.

**(d) Orthogonal projection and amplitudes.** Let
$\langle A,B\rangle:=h^{ac}h^{bd}A_{ab}B_{cd}$ on the subspace of tensors
spatial with respect to $n$. This is a positive definite inner product, and
for every spatial $A$ and every TT $B$, $\langle A-\Pi_{n,s}(A),B\rangle=0$;
so $\Pi_{n,s}$ restricted to the spatial tensors is the orthogonal projection
onto $T_{n,s}$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]],
[[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]). With respect to an
ordered $\eta$-orthonormal screen basis $(e_1,e_2)$ a TT tensor is

$$B=B_{11}\bigl(e^1\otimes e^1-e^2\otimes e^2\bigr)+B_{12}\bigl(e^1\otimes e^2+e^2\otimes e^1\bigr),$$

so $B$ is determined by the pair $(A_+,A_\times)=(B_{11},B_{12})$, and under
a screen rotation by $\theta$ this pair transforms as in
[[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]] clause (c); in particular the map
$T_{n,s}\to\mathbb R^2$, $B\mapsto(A_+,A_\times)$, is a linear isomorphism.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ and metric components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Since the chart identifies each
$T_p\mathbb R^4$ with $\mathbb R^4$, all objects below are defined by their
components in this chart; they are the components at a point, and a subscript
$p$ is suppressed. Indices are raised and lowered with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]), and orthogonality is in
the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]].

**(a) Observer, propagation direction, screen.** Let $n=n^a\partial_a$ be an
**observer** of the flat model: $n$ is future-directed, $\eta(n,n)=-1$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); and let
$s=s^a\partial_a$ be a **propagation direction**: $\eta(s,s)=1$ and
$\eta(n,s)=0$. The pair defines the two-dimensional **screen**
$\Sigma(n,s):=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:\eta(v,n)=0,\ \eta(v,s)=0\}$, on which the
restriction of $\eta$ is positive definite by
[[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The **screen projector** and
the **spatial projector** of the pair are the $(1,1)$-tensors with components

$$p^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b-s^as_b,\qquad h^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b,$$

and the covariant form of the screen projector is
$p_{ab}:=\eta_{ac}p^c{}_b=\eta_{ab}+n_an_b-s_as_b$. The properties $p^2=p$,
$h^2=h$, $\operatorname{im}p=\Sigma(n,s)$ and $\operatorname{im}h=n^\perp$
are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page.

**(b) TT projection.** Let $A=(A_{ab})$ be a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
at a point. Its **transverse-traceless (TT) projection with respect to
$(n,s)$** is the symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$\Pi_{n,s}(A)_{ab}:=p_a{}^cp_b{}^dA_{cd}-\tfrac12\,p_{ab}\,p^{cd}A_{cd},\qquad p^{cd}:=\eta^{ce}\eta^{df}p_{ef}.$$

**(c) Screen amplitudes.** Let $(e_1,e_2)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $\Sigma(n,s)$ (which exists by
[[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]] applied
to the positive-definite restriction of $\eta$). For a symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor $A$ the **plus and cross amplitudes of $A$ with respect to
$(e_1,e_2)$** are $A_+:=A(e_1,e_1)$ and $A_\times:=A(e_1,e_2)$; if $A$ is
TT with respect to $(n,s)$ in the sense of clause (d) below, then in the dual
basis $(e^1,e^2)$ of the screen

$$A=A_+\bigl(e^1\otimes e^1-e^2\otimes e^2\bigr)+A_\times\bigl(e^1\otimes e^2+e^2\otimes e^1\bigr).$$

For a TT screen tensor $A$, under the rotation
$e_1'=\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2$,
$e_2'=-\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2$ of the screen basis the amplitudes
transform as $A_+'=A_+\cos2\theta+A_\times\sin2\theta$ and
$A_\times'=-A_+\sin2\theta+A_\times\cos2\theta$. Here $\sin$ and $\cos$
are the power-series functions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]];
expanding $A(e_1',e_1')$ and $A(e_1',e_2')$ by bilinearity and applying the
addition formulas of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] gives the two
displayed transformations.

**(d) TT tensors and TT perturbations.** A symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
$A$ is **transverse-traceless (TT) with respect to $(n,s)$** when
$A(n,\cdot)=0$, $A(s,\cdot)=0$ and $\eta^{ab}A_{ab}=0$. For a symmetric
field $h$ on an open set of the flat model, "TT with respect to $(n,s)$"
means that these three conditions hold at every point. A symmetric field $h$
is **spatial with respect to $n$** when $h(n,\cdot)=0$ at every point.

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the screen, the two projections and the
amplitude terminology, and states the rotation law of clause (c) as part of
the naming. It asserts no property of $\Pi_{n,s}$ (idempotence, rank, image
and trace are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page), no relation
to the planar perturbations of the plane-wave definition of this page
(established in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page) and no physical
interpretation of the amplitudes.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the sets $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{im}T$ are
linear subspaces. Moreover, $T$ is injective if and only if $\ker T=\{0_V\}$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

- **(W1)** $0_V \in W$;
- **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies
  $u + v \in W$;
- **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: $\lambda \in F$ and
  $v \in W$ imply $\lambda v \in W$.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $U$ be a finite family of linear subspaces $U_i$ of
$V$ indexed by $i < n$ ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]); as everywhere on this page the index runs over
the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]).

**The sum of the other summands.** The set $\{0_V\}$ is a linear subspace of $V$:
it contains $0_V$, it is closed under addition since $0_V + 0_V = 0_V$, and it is
closed under scalar multiplication since $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]). So for each $j < n$ the family
$U^{(j)}$ defined by

$$U^{(j)}_i := U_i \quad (i \ne j), \qquad U^{(j)}_j := \{0_V\}$$

is again a finite family of linear subspaces of $V$ indexed by $i < n$, and we
write

$$\sum_{i \ne j} U_i \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} U^{(j)}_i ,$$

a linear subspace of $V$ by [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]. Replacing the
$j$-th summand by $\{0_V\}$, rather than re-indexing over a smaller set, keeps
every family on this page indexed by a natural number.

**The definition.** $V$ is the **internal direct sum** of the family $U$, written

$$V \;=\; \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i ,$$

when both of the following hold:

- **(D1)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i<n} U_i = V$;
- **(D2)** for every $j < n$,
  $\displaystyle U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$.

In (D2) the inclusion $\supseteq$ is automatic, since $U_j$ and
$\sum_{i \ne j} U_i$ are linear subspaces and each therefore contains $0_V$; the
content of (D2) is the inclusion $\subseteq$, that no nonzero vector of $U_j$ is
a sum of vectors drawn from the other summands.

### Two summands

Take $n = 2$ and write $U := U_0$, $W := U_1$. For $j = 0$ the family $U^{(0)}$ is
$\{0_V\}, W$, so $\sum_{i \ne 0} U_i = \{\, 0_V + w : w \in W \,\} = W$; for
$j = 1$ it is $U$ in the same way. So (D2) reduces to the single condition
$U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and

$$V = U \oplus W \quad\text{means}\quad U + W = V \ \text{ and } \ U \cap W = \{0_V\}.$$

For two summands, therefore, (D2) and the pairwise condition coincide; this is
the familiar form of the definition.

### Three or more summands: (D2) is not the pairwise condition

For $n \ge 3$ the condition (D2) is **strictly stronger** than requiring
$U_i \cap U_j = \{0_V\}$ for all $i \ne j$.

That (D2) implies the pairwise condition is immediate: for $i \ne j$ with
$i, j < n$ we have $U_i = U^{(j)}_i \subseteq \sum_{i \ne j} U_i$, since a sum of
a family contains each of its summands ([[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]]), so
$U_j \cap U_i \subseteq U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$, and the reverse
inclusion holds because both are linear subspaces.

The converse fails, and it fails already for three summands: a family can satisfy
(D1) and have all its pairwise intersections trivial while (D2) is false, so that
decompositions are not unique. The companion examples page records a witness. A
definition stated with the pairwise condition in place of (D2) would therefore be
a different, and weaker, notion, and the characterisation by unique decomposition
([[lem-direct-sum-criterion]]) would be false for it.

### The empty family

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so $n = 0$ is a genuine case. Then
$\sum_{i<0} U_i = \{0_V\}$ ([[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]) and (D2) is vacuous,
there being no $j < 0$. So $V = \bigoplus_{i<0} U_i$ holds exactly when
$V = \{0_V\}$: the zero space is the direct sum of the empty family, and no other
space is.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $V$ be a vector
space over $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $U$ be a family of linear subspaces
$U_i$ of $V$ indexed by $i < n$ ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]) with

$$V \;=\; \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$$

([[def-internal-direct-sum]]) and every $U_i$ finite-dimensional over $F$
([[def-dimension]]). Then $V$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and

$$\dim_F V \;=\; \sum_{i<n} \dim_F U_i ,$$

the right-hand side being the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read
additively in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{N}, +, 0)$
([[def-nat-addition]], [[lem-nat-add-identity]],
[[lem-nat-add-associative]], [[lem-nat-add-commutative]]).

**The base case is a genuine case.** At $n = 0$ the direct sum of the empty
family is $\{0_V\}$ and the empty sum of natural numbers is $0$, so the formula
reads $\dim_F\{0_V\} = 0$. **At $n = 2$** it reads
$\dim_F(U \oplus W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$.

**No choice principle is used.** The only inputs are
[[thm-dimension-formula]] and [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], both of
which are proved in finite dimension without one.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with additive identity $0_F$, multiplicative
identity $1_F$, and the field axioms as stated there. A **vector space over $F$**,
also called an **$F$-vector space**, consists of

- a set $V$, whose elements are called **vectors**;
- a binary operation $+ : V \times V \to V$ on $V$ ([[def-binary-operation]]),
  the **vector addition**;
- an element $0_V \in V$, the **zero vector**;
- a map $\cdot \,:\, F \times V \to V$, the **scalar multiplication**, written
  $\lambda v := \cdot(\lambda, v)$;

subject to the following axioms, in which $u, v \in V$ and $\lambda, \mu \in F$
are arbitrary.

- **(V1)** $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]): $+$ is associative
  and commutative, $0_V$ is a two-sided identity for $+$
  ([[def-identity-element]]), and every $v \in V$ has an additive inverse
  ([[def-invertible-element]]).
- **(V2)** $\lambda(u + v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$.
- **(V3)** $(\lambda + \mu)v = \lambda v + \mu v$.
- **(V4)** $(\lambda\mu)v = \lambda(\mu v)$.
- **(V5)** $1_F v = v$.

The elements of $F$ are called **scalars**. When several vector spaces are in
play we write $0_V$ for the zero of $V$, and we write $-v$ for the additive
inverse of $v$ and $u - v := u + (-v)$.

**The notation $0_V$ and $-v$ is legitimate.** Axiom (V1) asserts only that some
two-sided identity and some additive inverses exist. That there is at most one
two-sided identity for $+$ is [[lem-identity-unique]], and that an invertible
element of a monoid has exactly one inverse is [[lem-inverse-unique]]; both are
proved before [[def-group]] and are inherited here with the group structure. So
$0_V$ and $-v$ denote well-defined elements, and nothing below re-derives them.

**What (V1) buys, and why it is not restated.** Associativity, commutativity, the
identity law $v + 0_V = v = 0_V + v$, the inverse law $v + (-v) = 0_V$,
cancellation ([[lem-group-cancellation]]) and the inverse identities
([[lem-group-inverse-laws]]) are facts about abelian groups. They are quoted from
the group page wherever they are used and are never proved again for vectors.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

derivations.claim:
(Existence of the adapted frame.) A vector $n$ with $\eta(n,k)
eq0$ and the required properties exists: choose any future unit timelike $v$; if $\eta(v,k)
eq0$ take $n:=v$; if $\eta(v,k)=0$, nondegeneracy of $\eta$ and $k
eq0$ give a vector $w$ with $\eta(w,k)
eq0$, and for small $t
eq0$ the vector $v+tw$ is future timelike and has $\eta(v+tw,k)=t\eta(w,k)
eq0$; rescaling it to unit length gives $n$ by [L1]. Put $\omega:=-\eta(n,k)
eq0$ and $s:=\eta^{-1}(k)/\omega-n$, where $\eta^{-1}(k)$ is the vector with components $\eta^{ab}k_b$. Then $\eta(n,s)=\eta(n,k)/\omega-\eta(n,n)=(-\omega)/\omega+1=0$ and $\eta(s,s)=\eta(k,k)/\omega^2-2\eta(k,n)/\omega+\eta(n,n)=0-2(-\omega)/\omega-1=1$, so $s$ is a unit spacelike vector orthogonal to $n$; moreover $k=\omega(\eta(n,\cdot)+\eta(s,\cdot))$ by construction. By [L5] the pair extends to an $\eta$-orthonormal basis with $e_0=n$, $e_3=s$; in that basis the frame components of the covector are $k_A=k(e_A)=\omega(\eta(n,e_A)+\eta(s,e_A))=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ and the raised components are $k^A=\eta^{AB}k_B=\omega(1,0,0,1)$. This proves (a).

(The pure gauge amplitudes.) Let $H_{ab}=k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a$. Its trace is $\operatorname{tr}H=2k^aZ_a=:2\kappa_Z$, so $\bar H_{ab}=k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a-\eta_{ab}\kappa_Z$; hence $k^a\bar H_{ab}=k^ak_aZ_b+k^ak_bZ_a-k_b\kappa_Z=k_b\kappa_Z-k_b\kappa_Z=0$ because $k^ak_a=0$ and $k^ak_bZ_a=k_b\kappa_Z$. Thus $G\subseteq V_0$. If $H=0$, then testing in the frame of step 1.1 on $e_0$ gives $0=H(e_0,\cdot)=-\omega Z_\bullet+Z_0k_\bullet$; evaluating on $e_0$ gives $0=-2\omega Z_0$, so $Z_0=0$, and substituting back gives $\omega Z_b=0$ for every $b$, so $Z=0$. Hence $Z\mapsto(k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a)$ is injective, and its image $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R^4$, so $\dim G=4$ by [L3].

(The TT amplitudes.) If $X\in T$, then $\operatorname{tr}X=0$, so $\bar X=X$, and $X(e_0,\cdot)=X(e_3,\cdot)=0$; in frame components $k^a\bar X_{ab}=\omega(X_{0b}+X_{3b})=0$ for every $b$. Hence $T\subseteq V_0$. By [L2], $\dim T=2$. If $X\in T\cap G$ with $X=k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a$, then testing on $e_0$ as in step 2.1 gives $Z_0=0$ and then $Z=0$, so $X=0$: $T\cap G=\{0\}$.

(Solving for the TT representative.) Let $X\in V_0$ and let $Z$ be any vector. Define $X'_{ab}:=X_{ab}-k_aZ_b-k_bZ_a$. In frame components with $k_0=-\omega$, $k_3=\omega$, the four equations $X'_{0b}=0$ read $X_{0b}+\omega Z_b-k_bZ_0=0$, that is $$b=0:\ X_{00}+2\omega Z_0=0;\quad b=1:\ X_{01}+\omega Z_1=0;\quad b=2:\ X_{02}+\omega Z_2=0;\quad b=3:\ X_{03}+\omega Z_3-\omega Z_0=0,$$ whose unique solution is the displayed $Z$ (the matrix of the system is triangular with diagonal entries $2\omega,\omega,\omega,\omega$, all nonzero). Set $X'$ accordingly; then $X'\in V_0$ because $V_0$ is a subspace containing $X$ and $G$ (steps 2.1, 3.1). We show $X'\in T$. First, the harmonic-gauge condition $k^a\bar X'_{ab}=0$ in frame components reads $\omega(\bar X'_{0b}+\bar X'_{3b})=0$. For $b=1,2$ this is $X'_{31}+X'_{01}=0$ and $X'_{32}+X'_{02}=0$, because $\eta_{31}=\eta_{32}=0$; since $X'_{01}=X'_{02}=0$ by construction, $X'_{31}=X'_{32}=0$. For $b=0$ it gives $\bar X'_{00}+\bar X'_{30}=0$; here $\bar X'_{30}=X'_{30}-\tfrac12\eta_{30}\operatorname{tr}X'=X'_{03}=0$ and $\bar X'_{00}=X'_{00}-\tfrac12\eta_{00}\operatorname{tr}X'=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}X'$, so $\operatorname{tr}X'=0$. For $b=3$ it gives $\bar X'_{03}+\bar X'_{33}=0$ with $\bar X'_{03}=X'_{03}=0$ and $\bar X'_{33}=X'_{33}-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}X'=X'_{33}$, so $X'_{33}=0$. Substituting $\operatorname{tr}X'=X'_{11}+X'_{22}$ (which holds because $X'_{00}=X'_{33}=0$) gives $X'_{11}+X'_{22}=0$. Therefore $X'(e_0,\cdot)=0$, $X'(e_3,\cdot)=0$ and $\operatorname{tr}X'=0$: $X'\in T$.

(Uniqueness and the projection.) If $X'',X'$ are two TT representatives of the same $X$, their difference lies in $T\cap G=\{0\}$ by step 3.1 and the definition of $G$; so the representative is unique. Writing $\pi(X):=X'$, the assignment is the composition of the linear maps $X\mapsto(X,Z(X))$ and $(X,Z)\mapsto X-kZ-kZ$ with $Z$ the linear solution of step 4.1, hence linear; and $\pi(X)=X$ for $X\in T$ because then $Z=0$ solves $X'_{0b}=X_{0b}=0$ (uniqueness of the solution). Consequently every $X\in V_0$ is $X=\pi(X)+\bigl(X-\pi(X)\bigr)$ with $\pi(X)\in T$ and $X-\pi(X)\in G$, so $V_0=T+G$; combined with $T\cap G=\{0\}$ this is an internal direct sum, and by [L3] $\dim V_0=\dim T+\dim G=6$. The map $V_0/G\to T$, $X+G\mapsto\pi(X)$, is a linear isomorphism, and by [L2] the map $T\to\mathbb R^2$, $X\mapsto(X_{11},X_{12})$, is a linear isomorphism. This proves (b) and (c).

(Differential form and the gauge transformation.) For $h_{ab}=X_{ab}\cos(k\cdot x)$ we have $\bar h_{ab}=\bar X_{ab}\cos(k\cdot x)$ and, by [L4], $\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=k^a\bar X_{ab}(-\sin(k\cdot x))$; this vanishes identically exactly when $k^a\bar X_{ab}=0$ for every $b$, that is, exactly when $X\in V_0$. With $Z$ as in step 4.1 and $\xi_b=Z_b\sin(k\cdot x)$, the product rule and [L4] give $\partial_a\xi_b=k_aZ_b\cos(k\cdot x)$, hence $\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a=(k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a)\cos(k\cdot x)$ and $h'_{ab}=(X_{ab}-k_aZ_b-k_bZ_a)\cos(k\cdot x)=X'_{ab}\cos(k\cdot x)$ with $X'\in T\subseteq V_0$, so $h'$ is in harmonic gauge. This proves (d).

(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, 5.1 and 6.1 prove the four clauses; the arguments use finite linear algebra in an adapted orthonormal frame and the coordinate calculus of the flat model only. No field equation and no physical assumption enters, and no choice beyond the inherited countable choice of the cited finite-dimensional suppliers is used.

boundaries.evidence: statement clauses (b)-(c) and step 7.1: V_0 = T direct-sum G with dim V_0 = 6 and dim T = 2 by steps 3.1 and 4.1, so the quotient V_0/G is nonzero and no space in the statement is empty; the zero amplitude satisfies the equations with representative zero.

step 4.1: the frequency satisfies omega != 0, so the triangular system solved there has diagonal entries 2 omega, omega, omega, omega, all nonzero; for X = 0 the solution is Z = 0 and X' = 0, and step 5.1 shows the representative is unique with T intersect G = {0}.

boundaries.reason: No unit normalization or single-element case is claimed; the plane-wave gauge transformation Z and the frame are arbitrary within the proven formulas, and omega is an arbitrary nonzero frequency.

boundaries.evidence: statement clause (a) and step 1.1: the wave covector k is null and nonzero and the degenerate trial case eta(v,k) = 0 is handled explicitly by perturbing v with a vector w satisfying eta(w,k) != 0, which exists by nondegeneracy of eta; the resulting observer has eta(n,k) != 0.

boundaries.reason: All statements are pointwise linear-algebra identities at one cotangent datum of the flat model; no interval, endpoint or boundary limit occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and corresponding proof: steps 1.1 and 2.1 use one adapted orthonormal frame supplied by the finite-dimensional orthonormal-basis corollary and one arbitrary solution Z; no infinite selection is made and the arguments use only the inherited countable choice of the cited suppliers.

Statement (d) compares differential harmonic gauge with X in V_0. Step 6.1 writes the divergence as -k^a bar(X)_ab sin(k.x). Since k is nonzero, sin(k.x) is nonzero at some points, so an identically vanishing divergence forces each amplitude coefficient to vanish.

For X in V_0 all four coefficients k^a bar(X)_ab vanish by definition. Step 6.1 therefore makes the differential divergence zero at every x, proving harmonic gauge; its explicit differentiated sine gauge then preserves that condition.
