citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ ([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$u(x):=x^0-x^3$, $n:=du$, be the phase coordinate and wave covector of
[[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a); let $\Box$ be the flat
d'Alembertian of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). Then:

**(a)** The covector $n$ is nonzero and null, $\eta^{ab}n_an_b=0$, and its
spatial part has Euclidean norm $1$; the vector field
$T:=\partial_0+\partial_3$ is nonzero, null and future-directed, and
$\eta(T,\cdot)=-n$, so $n(T)=0$ and the wave covector
$k=\omega\,\eta(T,\cdot)$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a)
is the metric dual of $\omega T$, with components
$k_a=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ and $k^a=\omega(1,0,0,1)$. For $\omega>0$ this
vector is future null, for $\omega<0$ it is past null, and for $\omega=0$
it is zero and hence not null.

**(b)** For every $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function
$\varphi:=f\circ u$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^4$, and $T\varphi=0$ and
$\Box\varphi=0$ at every point.

**(c)** For every smooth map $F=(F_{ab}):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{4\times4}$
with values in the symmetric matrices, the planar perturbation
$h_{ab}(x):=F_{ab}(u(x))$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b)
is a smooth symmetric field with
$\partial_ch_{ab}=F'_{ab}(u)\,n_c$ and $\Box h_{ab}=0$ componentwise on
$\mathbb R^4$; moreover $(\partial_0+\partial_3)h_{ab}=0$. If in addition
the profile is TT, then $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$ and the divergence
$\eta^{bc}\partial_bh_{ac}$ vanishes componentwise.

**(d)** The profile is constant along the integral curves of $T$: for every
$x$ and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, $u(x+\sigma T)=u(x)$ and
$h_{ab}(x+\sigma T)=h_{ab}(x)$. Under the coordinate reparametrization
$t_c:=x^0/c$, these curves satisfy $|dx^3/dt_c|=c$. Here $c>0$ is only the
real parameter used in this mathematical coordinate change; no physical unit
or physical-time interpretation is asserted in this lemma.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),

$$\Bigl|\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_c\partial_a h^{c}{}_{b}+\partial_c\partial_b h^{c}{}_{a}-\Box h_{ab}-\partial_a\partial_b h\bigr).$$

**(c) Scalar curvature and Einstein tensor.** With the same constants,

$$\Bigl|S(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,S^{(1)}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad S^{(1)}=\partial_a\partial_bh^{ab}-\Box h,$$

and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,G^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h_{ab}+\partial^c\partial_{(a}\bar h_{b)c}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}.$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on
$\Omega$,

$$\bar h'{}_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a+\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\xi_c,\qquad \partial^a\bar h'{}_{ab}=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}-\Box\xi_b .$$

Consequently $h'$ is in harmonic gauge exactly when
$\Box\xi_b=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}$, and in that case

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h'{}_{ab}.$$

**(e) Gauge invariance of the first-order curvature.** For every smooth
covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h),\qquad S^{(1)}(h')=S^{(1)}(h),\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=G^{(1)}_{ab}(h).$$

That is, subtracting the pure-gauge perturbation
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a$ from the first-order perturbation leaves
the first-order Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors unchanged; their
first-order coefficients depend on $h$ only through its gauge-equivalence
class.

**(f) Quadratic remainder.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$ such that for every smooth symmetric component
field $A=(A_{ab})$ on a neighborhood of $K$ with

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^2\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|\le\delta_0,$$

the metric $\eta+A$ is Lorentzian of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $K$ and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+A)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)(p)\Bigr|\le \frac{C_K\,B_K(A)^2}{L^2}\qquad(p\in K),$$

where $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)$ is the right-hand side of the displayed formula of
(c) with $h$ replaced by $A$, and $G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ is the Einstein tensor of
the metric with components $\eta_{ab}+A_{ab}$.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $B$ be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space, and write $q(v):=B(v,v)$. The form is **positive definite** when $q(v)>0$ for every $v\ne0$, and **negative definite** when $q(v)<0$ for every $v\ne0$. The same terminology applies to the associated quadratic form.

Suppose a basis gives a diagonal matrix with $p$ positive diagonal entries, $q$ negative diagonal entries, and $r$ zero entries. Its **inertia** is the triple $(p,q,r)$, its **rank** is $p+q$, and its **signature** is $p-q$. Sylvester's law of inertia proves that this triple is independent of the diagonalizing basis, and therefore justifies the notation.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

A real $x$ is **positive** when it has a representative $(a_n)$ together
with a rational $\delta > 0$ and an index $N$ such that $a_n > \delta$
for all $n \ge N$. Define

$$x \le y \iff x = y \;\text{ or }\; y - x \text{ is positive},$$

and $|x| = x$ if $x \ge 0$, $|x| = -x$ otherwise.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),

$$\Bigl|\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_c\partial_a h^{c}{}_{b}+\partial_c\partial_b h^{c}{}_{a}-\Box h_{ab}-\partial_a\partial_b h\bigr).$$

**(c) Scalar curvature and Einstein tensor.** With the same constants,

$$\Bigl|S(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,S^{(1)}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad S^{(1)}=\partial_a\partial_bh^{ab}-\Box h,$$

and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,G^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h_{ab}+\partial^c\partial_{(a}\bar h_{b)c}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}.$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on
$\Omega$,

$$\bar h'{}_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a+\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\xi_c,\qquad \partial^a\bar h'{}_{ab}=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}-\Box\xi_b .$$

Consequently $h'$ is in harmonic gauge exactly when
$\Box\xi_b=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}$, and in that case

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h'{}_{ab}.$$

**(e) Gauge invariance of the first-order curvature.** For every smooth
covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h),\qquad S^{(1)}(h')=S^{(1)}(h),\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=G^{(1)}_{ab}(h).$$

That is, subtracting the pure-gauge perturbation
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a$ from the first-order perturbation leaves
the first-order Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors unchanged; their
first-order coefficients depend on $h$ only through its gauge-equivalence
class.

**(f) Quadratic remainder.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$ such that for every smooth symmetric component
field $A=(A_{ab})$ on a neighborhood of $K$ with

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^2\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|\le\delta_0,$$

the metric $\eta+A$ is Lorentzian of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $K$ and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+A)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)(p)\Bigr|\le \frac{C_K\,B_K(A)^2}{L^2}\qquad(p\in K),$$

where $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)$ is the right-hand side of the displayed formula of
(c) with $h$ replaced by $A$, and $G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ is the Einstein tensor of
the metric with components $\eta_{ab}+A_{ab}$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), so that at every $p\in M$ the form
$g_p$ has inertia $(3,1,0)$, and let $h$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) whose
support is compact.

**(a) Pointwise openness.** Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $4$
and let $G$ be a symmetric bilinear form on $V$ of inertia $(3,1,0)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). If in some basis of $V$ the matrix of $G$
has the form $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)+E$, then $G$ has inertia $(3,1,0)$
whenever $|E_{ij}|<1/8$ for all $i,j$. Consequently, for every basis the set
of matrices of symmetric forms of inertia $(3,1,0)$ is open in the space
$M_4^{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb R)$ with respect to the maximum-entry norm, and
equivalently $g_p$ has a neighborhood in the space of symmetric forms at $p$
consisting entirely of forms of inertia $(3,1,0)$.

**(b) Global stability.** There is $\lambda_0>0$ such that for every real
$\lambda$ with $|\lambda|<\lambda_0$ the smooth symmetric field $g+\lambda h$
is a smooth Lorentzian metric on $M$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with
time orientation inherited from $N$ (the field $N$ remains timelike for
$g+\lambda h$ for $|\lambda|$ small).

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ ([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$u(x):=x^0-x^3$, $n:=du$, be the phase coordinate and wave covector of
[[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a); let $\Box$ be the flat
d'Alembertian of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). Then:

**(a)** The covector $n$ is nonzero and null, $\eta^{ab}n_an_b=0$, and its
spatial part has Euclidean norm $1$; the vector field
$T:=\partial_0+\partial_3$ is nonzero, null and future-directed, and
$\eta(T,\cdot)=-n$, so $n(T)=0$ and the wave covector
$k=\omega\,\eta(T,\cdot)$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a)
is the metric dual of $\omega T$, with components
$k_a=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ and $k^a=\omega(1,0,0,1)$. For $\omega>0$ this
vector is future null, for $\omega<0$ it is past null, and for $\omega=0$
it is zero and hence not null.

**(b)** For every $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function
$\varphi:=f\circ u$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^4$, and $T\varphi=0$ and
$\Box\varphi=0$ at every point.

**(c)** For every smooth map $F=(F_{ab}):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{4\times4}$
with values in the symmetric matrices, the planar perturbation
$h_{ab}(x):=F_{ab}(u(x))$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b)
is a smooth symmetric field with
$\partial_ch_{ab}=F'_{ab}(u)\,n_c$ and $\Box h_{ab}=0$ componentwise on
$\mathbb R^4$; moreover $(\partial_0+\partial_3)h_{ab}=0$. If in addition
the profile is TT, then $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$ and the divergence
$\eta^{bc}\partial_bh_{ac}$ vanishes componentwise.

**(d)** The profile is constant along the integral curves of $T$: for every
$x$ and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, $u(x+\sigma T)=u(x)$ and
$h_{ab}(x+\sigma T)=h_{ab}(x)$. Under the coordinate reparametrization
$t_c:=x^0/c$, these curves satisfy $|dx^3/dt_c|=c$. Here $c>0$ is only the
real parameter used in this mathematical coordinate change; no physical unit
or physical-time interpretation is asserted in this lemma.

derivations.claim: (Lorentzian signature.) In the inertial chart the components of $g(\lambda)=\eta+\lambda h$ are $g_{00}=-1$, $g_{0i}=0$, $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+\lambda h_{ij}$. Since $h$ has nonzero components only at positions $11,22,12,21$ with $|h_{ij}|\le M$, for every $v\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ $$|v^iv^jh_{ij}|\le M\bigl((v^1)^2+(v^2)^2\bigr)+2M|v^1v^2|\le 2M\bigl((v^1)^2+(v^2)^2\bigr)\le2M|v|^2$$ by [F4], so $v^iv^j(\delta_{ij}+\lambda h_{ij})\ge(1-2M|\lambda|)|v|^2>0$ when $|\lambda|<1/(2M)$. The matrix of $g(\lambda)$ is therefore the orthogonal direct sum of the negative entry $-1$ and a positive definite $3\times3$ matrix; diagonalizing the latter gives three positive diagonal entries, so the inertia is $(3,1,0)$ and $g(\lambda)$ is a Lorentz form at every point by [F3]. The components are smooth by [F6] because $h$ has smooth components, so $g(\lambda)$ is a smooth Lorentzian metric; $g(\lambda)(\partial_0,\partial_0)=-1<0$ exhibits a smooth everywhere timelike vector field, which orients the metric by [F3], and $\partial_0$ is future-directed since $g(\partial_0,\partial_0)<0$ with the flat time orientation. This proves (a).

(Gauge, trace and wave equation.) For the TT profile $F$, the trace vanishes: $\eta^{cd}h_{cd}=h_{11}+h_{22}=A_+-A_+=0$, and $h_{00}=h_{01}=h_{02}=h_{03}=h_{33}=0$; hence $\bar h=h$. By [F1], $\partial^ah_{ab}=\eta^{ac}\partial_ch_{ab}=F'_{ab}(u)n^a$; for each $b$ this is $F'_{0b}(u)n^0+F'_{3b}(u)n^3$, with $n^0=-1$ and $n^3=-1$ by step 1.1 of [[lem-gr-null-phase-coordinate]], so it equals $-F'_{0b}(u)-F'_{3b}(u)=0$ because the profile satisfies $F_{a0}=F_{a3}=0$ for every $a$. Hence $\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0$: harmonic gauge. Also $\Box\bar h_{ab}=\Box h_{ab}=0$ for every $a,b$ by [F1]. By [F2] the first-order Einstein coefficient in harmonic gauge is $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)=-\tfrac12\Box\bar h_{ab}=0$; this is the linearized vacuum equation of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (e). The transversality for the wave covector is the vanishing of $\eta^{ac}k_ch_{ab}$ for every $b$: for the wave covector $k_c=\omega\eta_{cd}T^d$ with $T=\partial_0+\partial_3$ of [[lem-gr-null-phase-coordinate]] clause (a) this equals $\omega(h_{0b}+h_{3b})=0$ because the TT profile has $F_{0b}=F_{3b}=0$. This proves (b).

(Quadratic residual.) Fix the nonempty compact $K$ and $L>0$. Let $b_j$ be the supremum over $K$ of the maximum absolute value of the order-$j$ component derivatives of $h$, for $j=0,1,2$; these numbers are finite by [F4]. The quantity in clause (c) is $M_K=b_0+L^{-1}b_1+L^{-2}b_2$, while the supplier's control is $B_K(h)=b_0+Lb_1+L^2b_2$. Set $q_L:=\max\{1,L^2,L^4\}$. Termwise comparison gives $B_K(h)\le q_LM_K$ for every $L>0$. Take $\delta_0,C$ from [F5] for this nonempty $K$ and $L$, and choose $\lambda_0>0$ with $\lambda_0B_K(h)\le\delta_0$ and, when $M>0$, $\lambda_0<1/(2M)$; if $B_K(h)=0$, its constraint is automatic. For $|\lambda|\le\lambda_0$, put $A=\lambda h$, so $B_K(A)=|\lambda|B_K(h)\le\delta_0$. The metric is Lorentzian on all of $\mathbb R^4$ by step 1.1. Applying the residual estimate of [F5] on $K$ gives $|G_{ab}(\eta+\lambda h)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(\lambda h)(p)|\le C\lambda^2B_K(h)^2/L^2\le Cq_L^2\lambda^2M_K^2/L^2$. By linearity and step 2.1, $G^{(1)}_{ab}(\lambda h)=\lambda G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)=0$. Thus clause (c) holds with $C_K:=Cq_L^2<\infty$, also when $M_K=0$.

(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 prove clauses (a)-(c). Only the explicit components of the TT planar perturbation, the chain rule of [F1], the harmonic-gauge reduction of [F2] and the quadratic-remainder estimate of [F5] are used; no field equation is assumed, no source or matter model occurs, and no choice principle beyond the inherited countable choice of the cited suppliers is used.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. That $R_{abcd}$ are the components of a smooth $(0,4)$-tensor
field and that $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ are the components of a smooth
symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field, so that the contractions above are
basis-independent and do not depend on the chart, is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clauses (a)-(d); the Ricci symmetry
is part of that statement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),

$$\Bigl|\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_c\partial_a h^{c}{}_{b}+\partial_c\partial_b h^{c}{}_{a}-\Box h_{ab}-\partial_a\partial_b h\bigr).$$

**(c) Scalar curvature and Einstein tensor.** With the same constants,

$$\Bigl|S(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,S^{(1)}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad S^{(1)}=\partial_a\partial_bh^{ab}-\Box h,$$

and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,G^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h_{ab}+\partial^c\partial_{(a}\bar h_{b)c}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}.$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on
$\Omega$,

$$\bar h'{}_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a+\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\xi_c,\qquad \partial^a\bar h'{}_{ab}=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}-\Box\xi_b .$$

Consequently $h'$ is in harmonic gauge exactly when
$\Box\xi_b=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}$, and in that case

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h'{}_{ab}.$$

**(e) Gauge invariance of the first-order curvature.** For every smooth
covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h),\qquad S^{(1)}(h')=S^{(1)}(h),\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=G^{(1)}_{ab}(h).$$

That is, subtracting the pure-gauge perturbation
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a$ from the first-order perturbation leaves
the first-order Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors unchanged; their
first-order coefficients depend on $h$ only through its gauge-equivalence
class.

**(f) Quadratic remainder.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$ such that for every smooth symmetric component
field $A=(A_{ab})$ on a neighborhood of $K$ with

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^2\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|\le\delta_0,$$

the metric $\eta+A$ is Lorentzian of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $K$ and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+A)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)(p)\Bigr|\le \frac{C_K\,B_K(A)^2}{L^2}\qquad(p\in K),$$

where $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)$ is the right-hand side of the displayed formula of
(c) with $h$ replaced by $A$, and $G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ is the Einstein tensor of
the metric with components $\eta_{ab}+A_{ab}$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant

$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and

$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ ([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$u(x):=x^0-x^3$, $n:=du$, be the phase coordinate and wave covector of
[[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a); let $\Box$ be the flat
d'Alembertian of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). Then:

**(a)** The covector $n$ is nonzero and null, $\eta^{ab}n_an_b=0$, and its
spatial part has Euclidean norm $1$; the vector field
$T:=\partial_0+\partial_3$ is nonzero, null and future-directed, and
$\eta(T,\cdot)=-n$, so $n(T)=0$ and the wave covector
$k=\omega\,\eta(T,\cdot)$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a)
is the metric dual of $\omega T$, with components
$k_a=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ and $k^a=\omega(1,0,0,1)$. For $\omega>0$ this
vector is future null, for $\omega<0$ it is past null, and for $\omega=0$
it is zero and hence not null.

**(b)** For every $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function
$\varphi:=f\circ u$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^4$, and $T\varphi=0$ and
$\Box\varphi=0$ at every point.

**(c)** For every smooth map $F=(F_{ab}):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{4\times4}$
with values in the symmetric matrices, the planar perturbation
$h_{ab}(x):=F_{ab}(u(x))$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b)
is a smooth symmetric field with
$\partial_ch_{ab}=F'_{ab}(u)\,n_c$ and $\Box h_{ab}=0$ componentwise on
$\mathbb R^4$; moreover $(\partial_0+\partial_3)h_{ab}=0$. If in addition
the profile is TT, then $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$ and the divergence
$\eta^{bc}\partial_bh_{ac}$ vanishes componentwise.

**(d)** The profile is constant along the integral curves of $T$: for every
$x$ and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, $u(x+\sigma T)=u(x)$ and
$h_{ab}(x+\sigma T)=h_{ab}(x)$. Under the coordinate reparametrization
$t_c:=x^0/c$, these curves satisfy $|dx^3/dt_c|=c$. Here $c>0$ is only the
real parameter used in this mathematical coordinate change; no physical unit
or physical-time interpretation is asserted in this lemma.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),
