$k^A=\omega(1,0,0,1)$), both amplitude matrices have components
$X_{a0}=X_{a3}=Y_{a0}=Y_{a3}=0$ and $X_{11}+X_{22}=Y_{11}+Y_{22}=0$ in that
frame.

**(d) Screen amplitudes.** In the situation of (c) with
$k_A=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ in the adapted frame, the **screen** of $k$ is the two-dimensional linear
subspace $\Sigma_k:=\{v\in T_p\mathbb R^4:\eta(v,e_0)=\eta(v,e_3)=0\}$,
which is independent of the point $p$ and is the orthogonal complement of
$\operatorname{span}\{e_0,e_3\}$ in the sense of
[[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **plus and cross
amplitudes of a screen tensor** $A$ (a symmetric bilinear form on
$\Sigma_k$) with respect to an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2)$
of $\Sigma_k$ are $A_+:=A(e_1,e_1)$ and $A_\times:=A(e_1,e_2)$.

**(e) Linearized field equations.** Let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a real
parameter and let $S=(S_{ab})$ be a symmetric field on $\Omega$. A symmetric
field $h$ **solves the linearized field equation with source $S$ and
parameter $\Lambda$** when $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)+\Lambda h_{ab}=S_{ab}$ on
$\Omega$, with $G^{(1)}$ the first-order Einstein coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (b). It **solves the
linearized vacuum equations** when $S=0$ and $\Lambda=0$; and it **solves the
linearized vacuum equations with parameter $\Lambda$** when $S=0$ and
$\Lambda$ is arbitrary. A planar perturbation (b) or a plane wave (c) is a
**linearized vacuum wave** when it solves the linearized vacuum equations
with $\Lambda=0$.

**(f) Scope.** This item fixes objects and terminology only. It asserts no
existence of a profile or amplitude solving any equation, no relation between
the single-frequency and planar descriptions, and no physical
interpretation; in particular the harmonic-gauge condition in (c) is a named
algebraic condition whose equivalence with the differential condition of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (d) is proved in the
gauge-decomposition lemma of this page, and the terminology "TT" in (b)-(c)
is defined relative to a chosen orthonormal frame and not claimed to be
geometrically canonical.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $R$ be its
curvature ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let
$I,J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be intervals with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]), and let $F:J_0\times I\to M$ be a smooth map. Write
$T:=\partial_tF$ and $J^F:=\partial_rF$; a field along $F$ means a smooth
section of $F^*TM$ over $J_0\times I$, and $D_r,D_t$ are the covariant
derivatives in the two parameters
([[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Curvature as the commutator of the two derivatives.** For every smooth
field $V$ along $F$,
$$\bigl(D_tD_r-D_rD_t\bigr)V=R(T,J^F)V .$$

**(b) Geodesic deviation.** Suppose in addition that for every $r\in J_0$ the
curve $t\mapsto F(r,t)$ is a geodesic with affine parameter $t$, that is
$D_tT=0$. Then $D_tJ^F=D_rT$ and
$$D_t^2J^F=R(T,J^F)T .$$
Consequently, for every $r$ the field $t\mapsto J^F(r,t)$ is a Jacobi field
along the geodesic $t\mapsto F(r,t)$
([[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause (b)), and for a geodesic
variation the variation field is a Jacobi field.

**(c) Initial data.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth geodesic and let
$s_0\in I$. For every pair $J_0,J_1\in T_{\gamma(s_0)}M$ there exists exactly
one smooth Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$$J(s_0)=J_0,\qquad D_sJ(s_0)=J_1 .$$
The set of all Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ is a real vector space of
dimension $8$, and $J\mapsto\bigl(J(s_0),D_sJ(s_0)\bigr)$ is a linear
isomorphism onto $T_{\gamma(s_0)}M\oplus T_{\gamma(s_0)}M$.

**(d) The tangential component.** Let $\gamma$ be a smooth geodesic and $J$ a
smooth Jacobi field along it. Then $s\mapsto g(J,\gamma')(s)$ is affine, and
if $\gamma$ is future timelike with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-1$, the normal
component $J^\perp$ of [[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause
(e), explicitly $J^\perp=J+g(J,\gamma')\gamma'$, is again a Jacobi field
along $\gamma$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$R$ be its curvature ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Let
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized
geodesic with $D_s\gamma'=0$, written $T:=\gamma'$
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]); the parameter is the affinely
parametrized one of that definition and need not be proper time.

**(a) Fields along $\gamma$ and the derivative $D_s$.** A **field along
$\gamma$** is a section $J$ of the pullback bundle $\gamma^*TM$, and $D_s$
denotes the covariant derivative along $\gamma$ of
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. A field is **smooth** when its
coefficients in a smooth local frame of $M$ around each point of $\gamma$ are
$C^\infty$ on the corresponding parameter interval. At an included endpoint
of $I$ all derivatives below are one-sided.

**(b) Jacobi field.** A **Jacobi field along $\gamma$** is a smooth field $J$
along $\gamma$ satisfying the **Jacobi equation**
$$D_s^2J=R(T,J)T\qquad(s\in I),$$
that is $D_s^2J=R(\gamma',J)\gamma'$. The assignment
$J\mapsto R(T,J)T$, which associates with a field along $\gamma$ another
field along $\gamma$ and is $\mathbb R$-linear, is the **Jacobi operator of
$\gamma$**. Whether the field is smooth only piecewise is stated whenever a
statement uses piecewise fields; the unqualified term means globally smooth.

**(c) Geodesic variations.** A **geodesic variation with affine
parameter $s$** is a smooth map $F:J_0\times I\to M$, where
$J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with nonempty interior, such that
for every $r\in J_0$ the curve $s\mapsto F(r,s)$ is a geodesic with affine
parameter $s$. Its **variation field** is the field $s\mapsto\partial_rF(r,s)$
along the curve $s\mapsto F(0,s)$. The variation field of a geodesic
variation is a Jacobi field along that curve
([[thm-gr-jacobi-equation-and-geodesic-deviation]] clause (c)).

**(d) Conjugate instants and multiplicity.** Let $s_0<s_1$ be points of $I$.
The event $\gamma(s_1)$ is **conjugate to** $\gamma(s_0)$ **along $\gamma$**
when there is a nonzero Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$J(s_0)=J(s_1)=0$. In that case $s_1$ is called a **conjugate instant** of
$\gamma$ (with respect to $s_0$, when the base point needs to be named), and
the **multiplicity** of the conjugate instant is the dimension of the real
vector space of Jacobi fields vanishing at $s_0$ and $s_1$; the fields
vanishing at $s_0$ form a $4$-dimensional space and the multiplicity is at
most $4$, since a Jacobi field is determined by its value and derivative at
$s_0$ ([[thm-gr-jacobi-equation-and-geodesic-deviation]] clause (d)). For a
geodesic with $\gamma(s_0)=p$ and $\gamma'(s_0)=v$, the corresponding
possibility of conjugacy is measured by the derivative of the exponential
map at $s_1v$
([[lem-gr-conjugacy-via-the-exponential-map]]); that equivalence is proved,
not assumed here. No conjugate instant is asserted to exist.

**(e) The normal bundle.** If $\gamma$ is future timelike with
$g(T,T)=-1$, define its **normal bundle** to be the vector subbundle
$$N_\gamma:=\bigsqcup_{s\in I}N_\gamma(s)\subseteq\gamma^*TM,\qquad N_\gamma(s):=\{v\in T_{\gamma(s)}M:g_{\gamma(s)}(v,T(s))=0\}.$$
A **normal field** is a smooth section $J$ of $N_\gamma$, equivalently a
smooth field along $\gamma$ satisfying $g(J,T)=0$. Each fibre $N_\gamma(s)$
has dimension three, the restriction of $g_{\gamma(s)}$ to it is positive
definite, and $D_s$ maps normal fields to normal fields, since
$\frac{d}{ds}g(J,T)=g(D_sJ,T)+g(J,D_sT)=g(D_sJ,T)$ and $D_sT=0$; these
facts are proved in [[lem-gr-normal-index-form-factorization]] clause (b).
The norm of a normal field is $|J(s)|:=\sqrt{g_{\gamma(s)}(J(s),J(s))}$.
For any field $V$ along $\gamma$, its **normal component** is the field
$$V^\perp(s):=V(s)+g_{\gamma(s)}(V(s),T(s))\,T(s).$$
Indeed $g(T,T)=-1$ implies $g(V^\perp,T)=0$ and
$V=V^\perp-g(V,T)T$.

Adopt the postulates [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] of the classical gravitational
framework, and let $(M,g,N)$ be the model's smooth time-oriented Lorentzian
four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and curvature
$R$ ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). All statements below
are deductions within the model so specified; they assert nothing about
nature.

At an event $q$, a **frame** means an ordered basis
$(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ of $T_qM$. If an orthonormal frame is intended, it means
a tetrad satisfying $g_q(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$;
these terms and their distinction from coordinate frames are defined in
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Such a frame is pointwise basis
data, not a chart on an open set or an observer congruence, which is a smooth
future unit timelike vector field on an open set
([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]).

**(a) Free-fall congruences.** A **free-fall congruence** of the model is a
smooth map $\gamma:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times I\to M$, with
$\varepsilon>0$ and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an interval with nonempty interior,
whose values we write $\gamma(r,s)$. For each
$r\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ the curve $\gamma_r:I\to M$ is defined by
$\gamma_r(s):=\gamma(r,s)$ and is a future timelike geodesic parametrized by
proper time, with tangent field $U_r(s):=\partial_s\gamma(r,s)$ satisfying
$$g(U_r,U_r)=-c^2,\qquad D_sU_r=0,$$
where $D_s$ is the covariant derivative along $\gamma_r$.
By clause (ii) of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]], each $\gamma_r$ is
a worldline the model assigns to an ideal freely falling massive test body
with the corresponding release data, and conversely every such worldline
arises this way on its parameter interval. No injectivity or immersion
condition is imposed on the family map.

**(b) Deviation equation (model deduction).** Let $\gamma$ be a free-fall
congruence and set $J:=\partial_r\gamma$. Then, along each $\gamma_r$, the
separation field satisfies
$$D_s^2J=R(U_r,J)U_r,$$
where $D_s$ is the covariant derivative along $\gamma_r$. In particular, the
relative four-acceleration encoded by the family’s infinitesimal separation
field $J$ is exactly the curvature term: at each event,
$J\mapsto R(U_r,J)U_r$ is an $\mathbb R$-linear map on the event's tangent
space, vanishes at $J=0$, is tensorial and independent of the frame or chart
used for its components, and contains no rest mass, charge or
internal-structure parameter of the bodies.

**(c) Flat comparison and the vanishing criterion.** If the curvature
vanishes on an open subset $O\subseteq M$, then every free-fall congruence
with worldlines in $O$ has $D_s^2J=0$ there: the model predicts no tidal
relative acceleration of freely falling test bodies in that region.
Conversely, if at an event $q$ the operator $J\mapsto R(U,J)U$ vanishes for
every future timelike $U$ and every $J\in T_qM$, then $R_q=0$; hence within
the model the tidal response of all free-fall congruences detects exactly the
curvature, and $R$ is the model's complete tidal field at every event.

**Status.** Clauses (a)-(c) are conditional consequences of the stated
postulates and the cited mathematics. No observation, apparatus, measured
input or statistical inference is used; the item contains no empirical
premises, and the word "tidal" denotes the curvature term in the model's
deviation equation, not a measured force on any particular body.

For a given connection on $E$ and a smooth curve on an interval with nonempty interior, the **covariant derivative along the curve** is
$$D_tV=(\gamma^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial t}V.$$
Here $V$ is a section of the pullback bundle as in [[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]], and the pullback connection exists by [[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. It is real-linear and satisfies $D_t(fV)=f'V+fD_tV$ for functions of the parameter.

At an included endpoint the smooth up-to-boundary coefficients have their one-sided derivative; equivalently any smooth local extension of the coefficients gives this value, because extensions agreeing on a one-sided interval have the same derivative there. For a piecewise smooth curve the derivative is defined on each piece, with separate one-sided derivatives at corners; those derivatives are not required to agree. A singleton interval carries no derivative operator under this convention and will have identity transport by definition. A zero section or a rank-zero bundle gives zero covariant derivative. Constant base curves can have sections with nonzero coefficient derivative.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ ([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$u(x):=x^0-x^3$, $n:=du$, be the phase coordinate and wave covector of
[[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a); let $\Box$ be the flat
d'Alembertian of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). Then:

**(a)** The covector $n$ is nonzero and null, $\eta^{ab}n_an_b=0$, and its
spatial part has Euclidean norm $1$; the vector field
$T:=\partial_0+\partial_3$ is nonzero, null and future-directed, and
$\eta(T,\cdot)=-n$, so $n(T)=0$ and the wave covector
$k=\omega\,\eta(T,\cdot)$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a)
is the metric dual of $\omega T$, with components
$k_a=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ and $k^a=\omega(1,0,0,1)$. For $\omega>0$ this
vector is future null, for $\omega<0$ it is past null, and for $\omega=0$
it is zero and hence not null.

**(b)** For every $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function
$\varphi:=f\circ u$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^4$, and $T\varphi=0$ and
$\Box\varphi=0$ at every point.

**(c)** For every smooth map $F=(F_{ab}):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{4\times4}$
with values in the symmetric matrices, the planar perturbation
$h_{ab}(x):=F_{ab}(u(x))$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b)
is a smooth symmetric field with
$\partial_ch_{ab}=F'_{ab}(u)\,n_c$ and $\Box h_{ab}=0$ componentwise on
$\mathbb R^4$; moreover $(\partial_0+\partial_3)h_{ab}=0$. If in addition
the profile is TT, then $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$ and the divergence
$\eta^{bc}\partial_bh_{ac}$ vanishes componentwise.

**(d)** The profile is constant along the integral curves of $T$: for every
$x$ and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, $u(x+\sigma T)=u(x)$ and
$h_{ab}(x+\sigma T)=h_{ab}(x)$. Under the coordinate reparametrization
$t_c:=x^0/c$, these curves satisfy $|dx^3/dt_c|=c$. Here $c>0$ is only the
real parameter used in this mathematical coordinate change; no physical unit
or physical-time interpretation is asserted in this lemma.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart and let $(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over
an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with first-order coefficients
$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$ as in [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]]; write
$R^a{}_{bcd}(\lambda)$ for the curvature components of $g(\lambda)$
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]) and define the
**first-order curvature coefficient**

$$R^{(1)a}{}_{bcd}:=\partial_\lambda R^a{}_{bcd}(\lambda)\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad R^{(1)}_{abcd}:=\eta_{ae}R^{(1)e}{}_{bcd}.$$

Then:

**(a) General first-order formula.** The coefficient is defined (the
component family is differentiable in $\lambda$ at $0$) and

$$R^{(1)a}{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{cb},\qquad R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_b\partial_ch_{ad}+\partial_a\partial_dh_{bc}-\partial_a\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dh_{ac}\bigr).$$

**(b) Gauge invariance.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,
with $h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ the gauge-transformed
perturbation of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (d),
$R^{(1)}_{abcd}(h')=R^{(1)}_{abcd}(h)$: the first-order curvature coefficient
is unchanged by gauge transformations.

**(c) Planar and TT waves.** Let $F=(F_{ab})$ be a smooth planar profile with
$h_{ab}(x)=F_{ab}(u(x))$, $u=x^0-x^3$, and let $n_a=\partial_au$; then

$$R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\tfrac12\bigl(n_bn_cF''_{ad}+n_an_dF''_{bc}-n_an_cF''_{bd}-n_bn_dF''_{ac}\bigr).$$

If the profile is spatial ($F_{0a}=0$ for all $a$), then
$R^{(1)}_{0i0j}=-\tfrac12F''_{ij}$ and, raising indices,
$R^{(1)i}{}_{00j}=+\tfrac12F''{}^i{}_j$. If the profile is TT with amplitudes
$A_+,A_\times$, then $F''$ is supported on the screen with $F''_{11}=A_+''$,
$F''_{22}=-A_+''$, $F''_{12}=F''_{21}=A_\times''$ and all other second
derivatives of the profile zero; in particular

$$R^{(1)}_{0101}=-\tfrac12A_+'',\qquad R^{(1)}_{0102}=-\tfrac12A_\times'',\qquad R^{(1)}_{0202}=+\tfrac12A_+'' .$$

**(d) Contraction to the Ricci coefficient.** For every perturbation $h$,

$$\eta^{ac}R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{bd},$$

the right-hand side being the first-order coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (b). For a TT planar
perturbation both sides vanish: $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{bd}=0$ and
$S^{(1)}=0$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),

$$\Bigl|\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_c\partial_a h^{c}{}_{b}+\partial_c\partial_b h^{c}{}_{a}-\Box h_{ab}-\partial_a\partial_b h\bigr).$$

**(c) Scalar curvature and Einstein tensor.** With the same constants,

$$\Bigl|S(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,S^{(1)}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad S^{(1)}=\partial_a\partial_bh^{ab}-\Box h,$$

and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,G^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h_{ab}+\partial^c\partial_{(a}\bar h_{b)c}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}.$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on
$\Omega$,

$$\bar h'{}_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a+\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\xi_c,\qquad \partial^a\bar h'{}_{ab}=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}-\Box\xi_b .$$

Consequently $h'$ is in harmonic gauge exactly when
$\Box\xi_b=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}$, and in that case

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h'{}_{ab}.$$

**(e) Gauge invariance of the first-order curvature.** For every smooth
covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h),\qquad S^{(1)}(h')=S^{(1)}(h),\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=G^{(1)}_{ab}(h).$$

That is, subtracting the pure-gauge perturbation
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a$ from the first-order perturbation leaves
the first-order Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors unchanged; their
first-order coefficients depend on $h$ only through its gauge-equivalence
class.

**(f) Quadratic remainder.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$ such that for every smooth symmetric component
field $A=(A_{ab})$ on a neighborhood of $K$ with

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^2\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|\le\delta_0,$$

the metric $\eta+A$ is Lorentzian of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $K$ and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+A)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)(p)\Bigr|\le \frac{C_K\,B_K(A)^2}{L^2}\qquad(p\in K),$$

where $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)$ is the right-hand side of the displayed formula of
(c) with $h$ replaced by $A$, and $G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ is the Einstein tensor of
the metric with components $\eta_{ab}+A_{ab}$.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

A real $x$ is **positive** when it has a representative $(a_n)$ together
with a rational $\delta > 0$ and an index $N$ such that $a_n > \delta$
for all $n \ge N$. Define

$$x \le y \iff x = y \;\text{ or }\; y - x \text{ is positive},$$

and $|x| = x$ if $x \ge 0$, $|x| = -x$ otherwise.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart and let $c>0$ be the parameter of
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. All objects below are
component families in this chart.

**(a) Linearized-wave datum.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be a
nonempty open set and let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be a nonempty compact set. Fix a
length scale $L>0$, and use the numerical threshold $\delta_0=1/16$ and
chart control functional $B_K$ defined in
[[pthm-gr-linearized-field-equations]] clause (d) for this $K,L$. A
**linearized-wave datum on $K$** consists of:

- a flat linearized family $(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ over $\Omega$ with
  perturbation $h$ ([[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]]) such that
  $B_K(h)<\infty$ in the chart control functional of that clause;
- the real cosmological parameter $\Lambda$ and a smooth family
  $\mathcal T(\lambda)$ of stress-energy tensor fields on $\Omega$ for
  $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$, with component fields smooth
  jointly in $(\lambda,x)$ ([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]);
- the zeroth-order compatibility condition
  $\kappa\mathcal T_{ab}(0)=\Lambda\eta_{ab}$, where
  $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$; define the linearized source field, with curvature
  units, by $S_{ab}:=\kappa\,\partial_\lambda\mathcal T_{ab}(\lambda)|_0$,
  and require
  $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)+\Lambda h_{ab}=S_{ab}$ in the sense of
  [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (e);
- a nonzero real amplitude $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ for
  which $g(\lambda):=\eta+\lambda h$ is a Lorentzian metric of signature
  $(-,+,+,+)$ on a neighborhood of $K$.

The parameter $\lambda$ is dimensionless, and in the adopted SI length
coordinates $S_{ab}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)$ and $\Lambda h_{ab}$ have units
$\mathrm m^{-2}$, whereas $\mathcal T_{ab}$ has energy-density units and
$\kappa\mathcal T_{ab}$ has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]). The $B_K$ and $\delta_0$
values in the chart Taylor estimate are numerical controls: evaluate
component functions and their coordinate derivatives as SI numerical values
in this fixed length-coordinate chart, then form the displayed real-valued
functional. It is not a physical observable or an intrinsic norm. In this
fixed numerical convention, $B_K$, $\delta_0$ and $C_{K,L}$ are real control
numbers and $C_{K,L}B_K^2/L^2$ has the residual component unit
$\mathrm m^{-2}$ for $L$ in metres. The datum is a
**linearized vacuum wave datum** when $S=0$ and $\Lambda=0$. If in addition
the perturbation is a TT planar perturbation with amplitudes $A_+,A_\times$
([[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b)), the datum is a **TT
linearized-wave datum**. Its **approximation defect** is

$$D(\lambda,K):=\max_{a,b}\ \sup_{p\in K}\bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+\lambda h)(p)+\Lambda\,g_{ab}(\lambda)(p)-\kappa\,\mathcal T_{ab}(\lambda,p)\bigr|,$$

where $G$ is the Einstein tensor of the exact metric $\eta+\lambda h$;
this is the residual against the specified exact stress-energy family, not
against its first-order coefficient alone. In length coordinates it has
units $\mathrm m^{-2}$. The datum is **within the quadratic approximation**
when $|\lambda|B_K(h)\le\delta_0$. This uses the chosen threshold rather than
an unspecified existential $\delta_0/B_K(h)$, and also covers $B_K(h)=0$.
Whether a datum satisfies any of these conditions is a property of the
given data; this definition names the data, the condition and the defect and
asserts neither existence nor a bound.

**(b) Ideal two-body detector.** Let a TT linearized-wave datum be given.
Choose a nonempty open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a spatial point
$x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, and a nonzero spatial vector $\delta\in\mathbb R^3$
with Euclidean norm $|\delta|>0$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Require
the coordinate tube

$$\mathcal A_{J,\delta}:=\{(cs,\,x_0+q\delta):s\in J,\ q\in[0,1]\}$$

to lie in $\Omega$. For $q\in[0,1]$ define the smooth curves
$\gamma_q:J\to\Omega$ by $\gamma_q(s):=(cs,\,x_0+q\delta)$, and require
$g(\lambda)$ to be Lorentzian on a neighborhood of $\mathcal A_{J,\delta}$;
the
**reference worldline** is $\gamma_0$ and the **companion worldline** is
$\gamma_1$. Whenever these endpoint curves are the ideal freely falling
worldlines assigned by the postulate of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]],
their pair with $(x_0,\delta)$ is the **ideal two-body detector**. Its
**arm direction** is $e_\delta:=\delta/|\delta|$, the spatial unit vector in
the chosen inertial chart.

In SI length coordinates, the components of $x_0$ and $\delta$ and the arm
length $|\delta|$ are in metres, while $e_\delta$ is dimensionless.

**(c) Finite arm length and strain.** For $s\in J$ the prescribed spatial
arm path is $\sigma_s:[0,1]\to\Omega$, $\sigma_s(q):=\gamma_q(s)$, with
tangent $\dot\sigma_s(q)=\delta^i\partial_i$. Its **metric arm length** is
the metric length of this spacelike coordinate segment,

$$L_\delta(s):=\int_0^1\sqrt{g(\lambda)_{\sigma_s(q)}(\dot\sigma_s(q),\dot\sigma_s(q))}\,dq,$$

whenever the radicand is positive for every $q\in[0,1]$; the root is the
nonnegative square root of [[def-rational-power]]. This is the length along
the prescribed chart-straight path, not the infimum over spatial paths and
not a tangent-vector norm between finite-separated endpoints. The
**strain function** is $S_\delta(s):=L_\delta(s)/|\delta|-1$. For a TT
linearized-wave datum put

$$a_\delta(s,q):=\frac{\delta^i\delta^j h_{ij}(cs,\,x_0+q\delta)}{|\delta|^2}.$$

Since $g_{0i}=0$ and $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+\lambda h_{ij}$, wherever
$1+\lambda a_\delta(s,q)>0$ for every $q\in[0,1]$ one has

$$L_\delta(s)=|\delta|\int_0^1\sqrt{1+\lambda a_\delta(s,q)}\,dq,\qquad S_\delta(s)=\int_0^1\sqrt{1+\lambda a_\delta(s,q)}\,dq-1.$$

In the adopted SI length coordinates $L_\delta$ has units metres and
$S_\delta$ is dimensionless.

The **first-order strain response** is

$$S^{(1)}_\delta(s):=\left.\partial_\lambda S_\delta(s)\right|_{\lambda=0}=\tfrac12\int_0^1a_\delta(s,q)\,dq,$$

which is the parameter derivative of this finite-path length ratio; the
response theorem gives a uniform remainder estimate. If $\delta^3=0$, the
phase $u=cs-x_0^3-q\delta^3$ is constant along the arm, so the integrand is
constant in $q$ and the formula reduces to the usual single-point TT strain.

**(d) Reading and scope.** In the TT metric, $g(\gamma_q',\gamma_q')=-c^2$,
so $s=x^0/c$ is proper time along each endpoint curve; their geodesic and
free-fall properties are established in the response theorem of this page.
The detector is the two ideal endpoint bodies plus the defined path length
along a chosen coordinate segment at equal inertial-chart time; the length
depends on the chosen path and chart and is not asserted to be a geodesic
distance. Rigid bodies, elasticity, internal resonances, the propagation and
readout of light, noise and calibration are outside this definition; no
reading of a real apparatus is defined here, and no fact about nature is
asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ and metric components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Since the chart identifies each
$T_p\mathbb R^4$ with $\mathbb R^4$, all objects below are defined by their
components in this chart; they are the components at a point, and a subscript
$p$ is suppressed. Indices are raised and lowered with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]), and orthogonality is in
the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]].

**(a) Observer, propagation direction, screen.** Let $n=n^a\partial_a$ be an
**observer** of the flat model: $n$ is future-directed, $\eta(n,n)=-1$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); and let
$s=s^a\partial_a$ be a **propagation direction**: $\eta(s,s)=1$ and
$\eta(n,s)=0$. The pair defines the two-dimensional **screen**
$\Sigma(n,s):=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:\eta(v,n)=0,\ \eta(v,s)=0\}$, on which the
restriction of $\eta$ is positive definite by
[[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The **screen projector** and
the **spatial projector** of the pair are the $(1,1)$-tensors with components

$$p^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b-s^as_b,\qquad h^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b,$$

and the covariant form of the screen projector is
$p_{ab}:=\eta_{ac}p^c{}_b=\eta_{ab}+n_an_b-s_as_b$. The properties $p^2=p$,
$h^2=h$, $\operatorname{im}p=\Sigma(n,s)$ and $\operatorname{im}h=n^\perp$
are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page.

**(b) TT projection.** Let $A=(A_{ab})$ be a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
at a point. Its **transverse-traceless (TT) projection with respect to
$(n,s)$** is the symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$\Pi_{n,s}(A)_{ab}:=p_a{}^cp_b{}^dA_{cd}-\tfrac12\,p_{ab}\,p^{cd}A_{cd},\qquad p^{cd}:=\eta^{ce}\eta^{df}p_{ef}.$$

**(c) Screen amplitudes.** Let $(e_1,e_2)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $\Sigma(n,s)$ (which exists by
[[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]] applied
to the positive-definite restriction of $\eta$). For a symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor $A$ the **plus and cross amplitudes of $A$ with respect to
$(e_1,e_2)$** are $A_+:=A(e_1,e_1)$ and $A_\times:=A(e_1,e_2)$; if $A$ is
TT with respect to $(n,s)$ in the sense of clause (d) below, then in the dual
basis $(e^1,e^2)$ of the screen

$$A=A_+\bigl(e^1\otimes e^1-e^2\otimes e^2\bigr)+A_\times\bigl(e^1\otimes e^2+e^2\otimes e^1\bigr).$$

For a TT screen tensor $A$, under the rotation
$e_1'=\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2$,
$e_2'=-\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2$ of the screen basis the amplitudes
transform as $A_+'=A_+\cos2\theta+A_\times\sin2\theta$ and
$A_\times'=-A_+\sin2\theta+A_\times\cos2\theta$. Here $\sin$ and $\cos$
are the power-series functions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]];
expanding $A(e_1',e_1')$ and $A(e_1',e_2')$ by bilinearity and applying the
addition formulas of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] gives the two
displayed transformations.

**(d) TT tensors and TT perturbations.** A symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
$A$ is **transverse-traceless (TT) with respect to $(n,s)$** when
$A(n,\cdot)=0$, $A(s,\cdot)=0$ and $\eta^{ab}A_{ab}=0$. For a symmetric
field $h$ on an open set of the flat model, "TT with respect to $(n,s)$"
means that these three conditions hold at every point. A symmetric field $h$
is **spatial with respect to $n$** when $h(n,\cdot)=0$ at every point.

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the screen, the two projections and the
amplitude terminology, and states the rotation law of clause (c) as part of
the naming. It asserts no property of $\Pi_{n,s}$ (idempotence, rank, image
and trace are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page), no relation
to the planar perturbations of the plane-wave definition of this page
(established in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page) and no physical
interpretation of the amplitudes.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

The displayed geodesic is defined for every real $s$. By [A1] and the determination theorem, a physical freely falling test body with its release data follows its restriction to the body's actual proper-time interval. Steps 1.1-3.2 derive clauses (a)-(c) from the adopted postulates for the model spacetime and the cited mathematics; the only physical inputs are the clock and free-fall rules, and the only metric input is the explicit TT plane-wave family.
