citations.quote:
The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ ([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$u(x):=x^0-x^3$, $n:=du$, be the phase coordinate and wave covector of
[[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a); let $\Box$ be the flat
d'Alembertian of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). Then:

**(a)** The covector $n$ is nonzero and null, $\eta^{ab}n_an_b=0$, and its
spatial part has Euclidean norm $1$; the vector field
$T:=\partial_0+\partial_3$ is nonzero, null and future-directed, and
$\eta(T,\cdot)=-n$, so $n(T)=0$ and the wave covector
$k=\omega\,\eta(T,\cdot)$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (a)
is the metric dual of $\omega T$, with components
$k_a=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ and $k^a=\omega(1,0,0,1)$. For $\omega>0$ this
vector is future null, for $\omega<0$ it is past null, and for $\omega=0$
it is zero and hence not null.

**(b)** For every $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function
$\varphi:=f\circ u$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^4$, and $T\varphi=0$ and
$\Box\varphi=0$ at every point.

**(c)** For every smooth map $F=(F_{ab}):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{4\times4}$
with values in the symmetric matrices, the planar perturbation
$h_{ab}(x):=F_{ab}(u(x))$ of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b)
is a smooth symmetric field with
$\partial_ch_{ab}=F'_{ab}(u)\,n_c$ and $\Box h_{ab}=0$ componentwise on
$\mathbb R^4$; moreover $(\partial_0+\partial_3)h_{ab}=0$. If in addition
the profile is TT, then $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$ and the divergence
$\eta^{bc}\partial_bh_{ac}$ vanishes componentwise.

**(d)** The profile is constant along the integral curves of $T$: for every
$x$ and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, $u(x+\sigma T)=u(x)$ and
$h_{ab}(x+\sigma T)=h_{ab}(x)$. Under the coordinate reparametrization
$t_c:=x^0/c$, these curves satisfy $|dx^3/dt_c|=c$. Here $c>0$ is only the
real parameter used in this mathematical coordinate change; no physical unit
or physical-time interpretation is asserted in this lemma.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart and let $A_+,A_\times\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be bounded, with
$M:=\sup_{\mathbb R}\max\{|A_+|,|A_\times|\}$. Let $h$ be the TT planar
perturbation of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b) with these
amplitudes: $h_{11}(x)=A_+(u(x))$, $h_{22}(x)=-A_+(u(x))$,
$h_{12}(x)=h_{21}(x)=A_\times(u(x))$, and all other components zero, where
$u=x^0-x^3$. Let $\bar h_{ab}=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\eta_{ab}\eta^{cd}h_{cd}$ be the
trace reverse and $\Box$ the flat d'Alembertian of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). Then:

**(a) Small-amplitude metrics.** If $M>0$ and $|\lambda|<1/(2M)$, the field
$g(\lambda):=\eta+\lambda h$ with components
$g_{ab}(\lambda)=\eta_{ab}+\lambda h_{ab}$ is a smooth Lorentzian metric of
signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $\mathbb R^4$, and $\partial_0$ is a smooth
future-directed timelike vector field for it. If $M=0$, then $h=0$ and the
claim is trivial.

**(b) Harmonic gauge and wave equation.** The perturbation is traceless,
$\eta^{cd}h_{cd}=0$, so $\bar h=h$; it is in harmonic gauge,
$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0$ componentwise; and $\Box\bar h_{ab}=0$
componentwise. Hence the first-order Einstein coefficient vanishes,
$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)=0$: $h$ solves the linearized vacuum equations in the sense
of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (e), and it is transverse for
the wave covector of clause (a) of that definition.

**(c) Quadratic residual.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be a nonempty compact set and let
$L>0$. With
$M_K:=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|h_{ab}|+L^{-1}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_ch_{ab}|+L^{-2}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dh_{ab}|$,
there are $\lambda_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$, depending on $K$, $h$, $L$ but not
on $\lambda$, such that for every $|\lambda|\le\lambda_0$ the metric
$\eta+\lambda h$ is Lorentzian on $K$ and

$$\bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+\lambda h)(p)\bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2 M_K^2/L^2\qquad(p\in K,\ a,b=0,1,2,3),$$

where $G_{ab}$ is the Einstein tensor of the truncated metric $\eta+\lambda h$.
This is an estimate for the mathematical tensor $G$ in the stated chart norm;
it makes no physical field-law claim.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ and constant metric components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$
be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under the chart; all
components and all partial derivatives below are taken in this chart. Let
$c>0$ be a real parameter. Throughout, a **symmetric field** means a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $\Omega$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) and indices are raised and
lowered with $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{-1}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]).

**(a) Phase coordinate and wave covector.** The **phase coordinate** of the
planar waves of this page is $u(x):=x^0-x^3$. Its differential $n:=du$ has
components $n_a=\delta^0_a-\delta^3_a$, so that $n_0=1$, $n_3=-1$,
$n_1=n_2=0$ and $\eta^{ab}n_an_b=-1+1=0$: $n$ is a nonzero null covector, and
the vector with spatial components $(0,0,-1)$ has Euclidean norm $1$ in the
sense of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The vector $T:=\partial_0+\partial_3$
is null and future-directed, and $\eta(T,\cdot)=-n$, so that the phase
covector is the metric dual of $-T$. For $\omega\in\mathbb R$ we call
$k_a:=\omega\,\eta_{ab}T^b=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ a **wave covector**; $\omega$
is its real phase coefficient and $|\omega|$ its absolute value. Its raised components are $k^a=\omega T^a=
\omega(1,0,0,1)$, so that $k\ne0$ for $\omega\ne0$ and $k^ak_a=0$. For a
general null covector $k\ne0$ of the flat model the adapted orthonormal
frames are treated in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page; clauses
(a)-(d) fix the standard propagation direction $x^3$ used on this page.

**(b) Planar perturbations and TT profiles.** A symmetric field $h$ on
$\Omega$ is a **planar perturbation** when there is a smooth map
$F=(F_{ab}):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{4\times4}$ with values in the symmetric
matrices such that $h_{ab}(x)=F_{ab}(u(x))$ for all $x\in\Omega$; such an
$F$ is a **planar profile**. The image $u(\Omega)$ is open: near each
$x\in\Omega$, varying $x^0$ through a sufficiently small interval varies
$u(x)$ through an interval while remaining in $\Omega$. The restriction
$F|_{u(\Omega)}$ is uniquely determined by $h$, but an extension of it outside
$u(\Omega)$ is not determined unless $u(\Omega)=\mathbb R$. A planar
perturbation is **transverse traceless (TT) with respect to the inertial
frame** when $h_{a0}=h_{a3}=0$ and $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$;
equivalently, a chosen profile satisfies $F_{a0}=F_{a3}=0$ and
$F_{11}+F_{22}=0$ on $u(\Omega)$. In that case its restriction to
$u(\Omega)$ has the form

$$F_{ab}(u)=A_+(u)\bigl(\delta^1_a\delta^1_b-\delta^2_a\delta^2_b\bigr)+A_\times(u)\bigl(\delta^1_a\delta^2_b+\delta^2_a\delta^1_b\bigr)$$

for smooth functions $A_+,A_\times:u(\Omega)\to\mathbb R$, uniquely given by
$A_+=F_{11}|_{u(\Omega)}$ and $A_\times=F_{12}|_{u(\Omega)}$; these are the
**plus and cross amplitudes** on the phase image. In particular a TT planar perturbation is
spatial ($h_{a0}=0$), traceless ($\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$) and transverse (its
contraction with the wave covector of (a) vanishes).

**(c) Single-frequency plane waves.** Let $k\ne0$ be a null covector of the
flat model and let $X=(X_{ab})$ and $Y=(Y_{ab})$ be real symmetric matrices.
The symmetric field

$$h_{ab}(x):=X_{ab}\cos(k\cdot x)+Y_{ab}\sin(k\cdot x),\qquad k\cdot x:=k_ax^a,$$

where $\cos$ and $\sin$ are the power-series functions
([[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]), is the **plane-wave perturbation
with wave covector $k$ and amplitudes $(X,Y)$**. Its **trace-reversed
amplitudes** are $\bar X_{ab}:=X_{ab}-\tfrac12\eta_{ab}\eta^{cd}X_{cd}$ and
$\bar Y_{ab}:=Y_{ab}-\tfrac12\eta_{ab}\eta^{cd}Y_{cd}$, in agreement with the
trace reversal of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). The
plane wave is **in harmonic gauge** when $k^a\bar X_{ab}=0$ and
$k^a\bar Y_{ab}=0$. The plane wave is **TT with respect to the wave covector
$k$** when, in some $\eta$-orthonormal frame $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0$
future timelike, $e_1,e_2$ spanning the screen of (d) and
$k_A=k(e_A)=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ for some $\omega\ne0$ (existence of such a
frame is proved in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page, where also
$k^A=\omega(1,0,0,1)$), both amplitude matrices have components
$X_{a0}=X_{a3}=Y_{a0}=Y_{a3}=0$ and $X_{11}+X_{22}=Y_{11}+Y_{22}=0$ in that
frame.

**(d) Screen amplitudes.** In the situation of (c) with
$k_A=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ in the adapted frame, the **screen** of $k$ is the two-dimensional linear
subspace $\Sigma_k:=\{v\in T_p\mathbb R^4:\eta(v,e_0)=\eta(v,e_3)=0\}$,
which is independent of the point $p$ and is the orthogonal complement of
$\operatorname{span}\{e_0,e_3\}$ in the sense of
[[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **plus and cross
amplitudes of a screen tensor** $A$ (a symmetric bilinear form on
$\Sigma_k$) with respect to an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2)$
of $\Sigma_k$ are $A_+:=A(e_1,e_1)$ and $A_\times:=A(e_1,e_2)$.

**(e) Linearized field equations.** Let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a real
parameter and let $S=(S_{ab})$ be a symmetric field on $\Omega$. A symmetric
field $h$ **solves the linearized field equation with source $S$ and
parameter $\Lambda$** when $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)+\Lambda h_{ab}=S_{ab}$ on
$\Omega$, with $G^{(1)}$ the first-order Einstein coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (b). It **solves the
linearized vacuum equations** when $S=0$ and $\Lambda=0$; and it **solves the
linearized vacuum equations with parameter $\Lambda$** when $S=0$ and
$\Lambda$ is arbitrary. A planar perturbation (b) or a plane wave (c) is a
**linearized vacuum wave** when it solves the linearized vacuum equations
with $\Lambda=0$.

**(f) Scope.** This item fixes objects and terminology only. It asserts no
existence of a profile or amplitude solving any equation, no relation between
the single-frequency and planar descriptions, and no physical
interpretation; in particular the harmonic-gauge condition in (c) is a named
algebraic condition whose equivalence with the differential condition of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (d) is proved in the
gauge-decomposition lemma of this page, and the terminology "TT" in (b)-(c)
is defined relative to a chosen orthonormal frame and not claimed to be
geometrically canonical.

Adopt the field-law postulate [[post-gr-einstein-field-law]] with its
constants $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, $G_N>0$, $c>0$, together with
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]]
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]). Let
$(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its inertial
chart, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be a nonempty open set, let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
$\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon$, and let
$(T(\lambda))_{\lambda\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)}$ be a family of smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor fields on $\Omega$ whose component families
$T_{ab}(\lambda,p)$ are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ and such that for every
$\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$ the pair $(g(\lambda),T(\lambda))$
satisfies the adopted field law

$$G_{ab}\bigl(g(\lambda)\bigr)+\Lambda\,g_{ab}(\lambda)=\kappa\,T_{ab}(\lambda)\qquad\text{on }\Omega,\qquad \kappa:=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4},$$

$G$ being the Einstein tensor of the metric-selected connection
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]). Define
$T^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda T_{ab}(\lambda)\big|_{\lambda=0}$. Then:

**(a) Linearized field equation with source.** On $\Omega$,

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)+\Lambda\,h_{ab}=\kappa\,T^{(1)}_{ab},$$

where $G^{(1)}$ is the first-order Einstein coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]]. In particular the linearized
equation of the model is not an independent postulate: it is the first-order
consequence of the adopted field law along the family.

**(b) Vacuum and harmonic-gauge reduction.** If $T(\lambda)=0$ for every
$\lambda$ and $\Lambda=0$, then $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)=0$; if in addition $h$
satisfies the harmonic-gauge condition $\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0$
([[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (d)), then
$\Box\bar h_{ab}=0$ componentwise on $\Omega$.

**(c) Sourced wave equation in harmonic gauge.** If $h$ is in harmonic gauge
and solves the linearized equation with source $S$ and parameter $\Lambda$ in
the sense of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (e), then
$\Box\bar h_{ab}=2\Lambda h_{ab}-2S_{ab}$ on $\Omega$.

**(d) Quadratic residual of a linearized vacuum wave.** Let
$K\subseteq\Omega$ be a nonempty compact set and let $L>0$ be a length scale. In the fixed
SI numerical chart define the real control functional

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L^{-1}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^{-2}\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|.$$

Take the fixed dimensionless numerical threshold $\delta_0:=1/16$. If $h$ is
a smooth symmetric perturbation on a neighborhood of $K$ with
$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)=0$ on $K$, then there is a finite dimensionless numerical
constant $C_{K,L}$ such that, for every real $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|B_K(h)\le\delta_0$,

$$\bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+\lambda h)(p)\bigr|\le C_{K,L}\,\lambda^2B_K(h)^2/L^2\qquad(p\in K).$$

The functional $B_K$ and threshold are numerical chart controls, not physical
observables; each component and derivative is first evaluated in the fixed
SI length-coordinate convention. With $L$ in metres, the displayed residual
has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$. For the zero-source branch $T(\lambda)=0$ with
$\Lambda=0$, this bounds the residual of the exact vacuum field law on $K$.

**(e) All-space harmonic gauge (assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$).** If
$\Omega=\mathbb R^4$, $h$ solves the linearized vacuum equations with
$\Lambda=0$, and the Axiom of Countable Choice is assumed
([[def-countable-choice]]), then there is a smooth covector
field $\xi$ on $\mathbb R^4$ such that
$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ is in harmonic gauge,
$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=0$ and $\Box\bar h'_{ab}=0$ componentwise.

**Status.** Clauses (a)-(e) are conditional deductions from the adopted field
law and the cited mathematics for the stated families; they assert no
observation, no measured constant and no fact about nature. The item contains
no empirical premise.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart and let $c>0$ be the parameter of
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. All objects below are
component families in this chart.

**(a) Linearized-wave datum.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be a
nonempty open set and let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be a nonempty compact set. Fix a
length scale $L>0$, and use the numerical threshold $\delta_0=1/16$ and
chart control functional $B_K$ defined in
[[pthm-gr-linearized-field-equations]] clause (d) for this $K,L$. A
**linearized-wave datum on $K$** consists of:

- a flat linearized family $(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ over $\Omega$ with
  perturbation $h$ ([[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]]) such that
  $B_K(h)<\infty$ in the chart control functional of that clause;
- the real cosmological parameter $\Lambda$ and a smooth family
  $\mathcal T(\lambda)$ of stress-energy tensor fields on $\Omega$ for
  $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$, with component fields smooth
  jointly in $(\lambda,x)$ ([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]);
- the zeroth-order compatibility condition
  $\kappa\mathcal T_{ab}(0)=\Lambda\eta_{ab}$, where
  $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$; define the linearized source field, with curvature
  units, by $S_{ab}:=\kappa\,\partial_\lambda\mathcal T_{ab}(\lambda)|_0$,
  and require
  $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)+\Lambda h_{ab}=S_{ab}$ in the sense of
  [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (e);
- a nonzero real amplitude $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ for
  which $g(\lambda):=\eta+\lambda h$ is a Lorentzian metric of signature
  $(-,+,+,+)$ on a neighborhood of $K$.

The parameter $\lambda$ is dimensionless, and in the adopted SI length
coordinates $S_{ab}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)$ and $\Lambda h_{ab}$ have units
$\mathrm m^{-2}$, whereas $\mathcal T_{ab}$ has energy-density units and
$\kappa\mathcal T_{ab}$ has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]). The $B_K$ and $\delta_0$
values in the chart Taylor estimate are numerical controls: evaluate
component functions and their coordinate derivatives as SI numerical values
in this fixed length-coordinate chart, then form the displayed real-valued
functional. It is not a physical observable or an intrinsic norm. In this
fixed numerical convention, $B_K$, $\delta_0$ and $C_{K,L}$ are real control
numbers and $C_{K,L}B_K^2/L^2$ has the residual component unit
$\mathrm m^{-2}$ for $L$ in metres. The datum is a
**linearized vacuum wave datum** when $S=0$ and $\Lambda=0$. If in addition
the perturbation is a TT planar perturbation with amplitudes $A_+,A_\times$
([[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (b)), the datum is a **TT
linearized-wave datum**. Its **approximation defect** is

$$D(\lambda,K):=\max_{a,b}\ \sup_{p\in K}\bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+\lambda h)(p)+\Lambda\,g_{ab}(\lambda)(p)-\kappa\,\mathcal T_{ab}(\lambda,p)\bigr|,$$

where $G$ is the Einstein tensor of the exact metric $\eta+\lambda h$;
this is the residual against the specified exact stress-energy family, not
against its first-order coefficient alone. In length coordinates it has
units $\mathrm m^{-2}$. The datum is **within the quadratic approximation**
when $|\lambda|B_K(h)\le\delta_0$. This uses the chosen threshold rather than
an unspecified existential $\delta_0/B_K(h)$, and also covers $B_K(h)=0$.
Whether a datum satisfies any of these conditions is a property of the
given data; this definition names the data, the condition and the defect and
asserts neither existence nor a bound.

**(b) Ideal two-body detector.** Let a TT linearized-wave datum be given.
Choose a nonempty open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a spatial point
$x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, and a nonzero spatial vector $\delta\in\mathbb R^3$
with Euclidean norm $|\delta|>0$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Require
the coordinate tube

$$\mathcal A_{J,\delta}:=\{(cs,\,x_0+q\delta):s\in J,\ q\in[0,1]\}$$

to lie in $\Omega$. For $q\in[0,1]$ define the smooth curves
$\gamma_q:J\to\Omega$ by $\gamma_q(s):=(cs,\,x_0+q\delta)$, and require
$g(\lambda)$ to be Lorentzian on a neighborhood of $\mathcal A_{J,\delta}$;
the
**reference worldline** is $\gamma_0$ and the **companion worldline** is
$\gamma_1$. Whenever these endpoint curves are the ideal freely falling
worldlines assigned by the postulate of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]],
their pair with $(x_0,\delta)$ is the **ideal two-body detector**. Its
**arm direction** is $e_\delta:=\delta/|\delta|$, the spatial unit vector in
the chosen inertial chart.

In SI length coordinates, the components of $x_0$ and $\delta$ and the arm
length $|\delta|$ are in metres, while $e_\delta$ is dimensionless.

**(c) Finite arm length and strain.** For $s\in J$ the prescribed spatial
arm path is $\sigma_s:[0,1]\to\Omega$, $\sigma_s(q):=\gamma_q(s)$, with
tangent $\dot\sigma_s(q)=\delta^i\partial_i$. Its **metric arm length** is
the metric length of this spacelike coordinate segment,

$$L_\delta(s):=\int_0^1\sqrt{g(\lambda)_{\sigma_s(q)}(\dot\sigma_s(q),\dot\sigma_s(q))}\,dq,$$

whenever the radicand is positive for every $q\in[0,1]$; the root is the
nonnegative square root of [[def-rational-power]]. This is the length along
the prescribed chart-straight path, not the infimum over spatial paths and
not a tangent-vector norm between finite-separated endpoints. The
**strain function** is $S_\delta(s):=L_\delta(s)/|\delta|-1$. For a TT
linearized-wave datum put

$$a_\delta(s,q):=\frac{\delta^i\delta^j h_{ij}(cs,\,x_0+q\delta)}{|\delta|^2}.$$

Since $g_{0i}=0$ and $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+\lambda h_{ij}$, wherever
$1+\lambda a_\delta(s,q)>0$ for every $q\in[0,1]$ one has

$$L_\delta(s)=|\delta|\int_0^1\sqrt{1+\lambda a_\delta(s,q)}\,dq,\qquad S_\delta(s)=\int_0^1\sqrt{1+\lambda a_\delta(s,q)}\,dq-1.$$

In the adopted SI length coordinates $L_\delta$ has units metres and
$S_\delta$ is dimensionless.

The **first-order strain response** is

$$S^{(1)}_\delta(s):=\left.\partial_\lambda S_\delta(s)\right|_{\lambda=0}=\tfrac12\int_0^1a_\delta(s,q)\,dq,$$

which is the parameter derivative of this finite-path length ratio; the
response theorem gives a uniform remainder estimate. If $\delta^3=0$, the
phase $u=cs-x_0^3-q\delta^3$ is constant along the arm, so the integrand is
constant in $q$ and the formula reduces to the usual single-point TT strain.

**(d) Reading and scope.** In the TT metric, $g(\gamma_q',\gamma_q')=-c^2$,
so $s=x^0/c$ is proper time along each endpoint curve; their geodesic and
free-fall properties are established in the response theorem of this page.
The detector is the two ideal endpoint bodies plus the defined path length
along a chosen coordinate segment at equal inertial-chart time; the length
depends on the chosen path and chart and is not asserted to be a geodesic
distance. Rigid bodies, elasticity, internal resonances, the propagation and
readout of light, noise and calibration are outside this definition; no
reading of a real apparatus is defined here, and no fact about nature is
asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart and let $(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over
an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with first-order coefficients
$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$ as in [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]]; write
$R^a{}_{bcd}(\lambda)$ for the curvature components of $g(\lambda)$
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]) and define the
**first-order curvature coefficient**

$$R^{(1)a}{}_{bcd}:=\partial_\lambda R^a{}_{bcd}(\lambda)\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad R^{(1)}_{abcd}:=\eta_{ae}R^{(1)e}{}_{bcd}.$$

Then:

**(a) General first-order formula.** The coefficient is defined (the
component family is differentiable in $\lambda$ at $0$) and

$$R^{(1)a}{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{cb},\qquad R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_b\partial_ch_{ad}+\partial_a\partial_dh_{bc}-\partial_a\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dh_{ac}\bigr).$$

**(b) Gauge invariance.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,
with $h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ the gauge-transformed
perturbation of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (d),
$R^{(1)}_{abcd}(h')=R^{(1)}_{abcd}(h)$: the first-order curvature coefficient
is unchanged by gauge transformations.

**(c) Planar and TT waves.** Let $F=(F_{ab})$ be a smooth planar profile with
$h_{ab}(x)=F_{ab}(u(x))$, $u=x^0-x^3$, and let $n_a=\partial_au$; then

$$R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\tfrac12\bigl(n_bn_cF''_{ad}+n_an_dF''_{bc}-n_an_cF''_{bd}-n_bn_dF''_{ac}\bigr).$$

If the profile is spatial ($F_{0a}=0$ for all $a$), then
$R^{(1)}_{0i0j}=-\tfrac12F''_{ij}$ and, raising indices,
$R^{(1)i}{}_{00j}=+\tfrac12F''{}^i{}_j$. If the profile is TT with amplitudes
$A_+,A_\times$, then $F''$ is supported on the screen with $F''_{11}=A_+''$,
$F''_{22}=-A_+''$, $F''_{12}=F''_{21}=A_\times''$ and all other second
derivatives of the profile zero; in particular

$$R^{(1)}_{0101}=-\tfrac12A_+'',\qquad R^{(1)}_{0102}=-\tfrac12A_\times'',\qquad R^{(1)}_{0202}=+\tfrac12A_+'' .$$

**(d) Contraction to the Ricci coefficient.** For every perturbation $h$,

$$\eta^{ac}R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{bd},$$

the right-hand side being the first-order coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (b). For a TT planar
perturbation both sides vanish: $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{bd}=0$ and
$S^{(1)}=0$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

derivations.claim: (Second derivatives.) Differentiating twice in $x^0$ with [L1], $A_+''(u)=-\omega^2a\cos(\omega u)$ and $A_\times''(u)=-\omega^2b\sin(\omega u)$. Hence $h$ has smooth bounded profiles with bound $M$, and clause 1 is [L2].

(Curvature components.) By [L3], $R^{(1)}_{0101}=-\tfrac12F''_{11}=-\tfrac12A_+''=\tfrac12a\omega^2\cos(\omega u)$, $R^{(1)}_{0102}=-\tfrac12F''_{12}=-\tfrac12A_\times''=\tfrac12b\omega^2\sin(\omega u)$ and $R^{(1)}_{0202}=-\tfrac12F''_{22}=\tfrac12A_+''=-\tfrac12a\omega^2\cos(\omega u)$; the vanishing for $i=3$ or $j=3$ is part of the same clause. This proves clause 2.

(Curvature and general-phase strain.) At $u=0$, $\cos0=1$ and $\sin0=0$, so the displayed curvature values are $\tfrac12a\omega^2$ and $0$. For $\delta=|\delta|e_1$, $\delta^3=0$, the profile is constant along the arm and $a(s,q)=A_+(u)=a\cos(\omega u)$, so the exact strain is $\sqrt{1+\lambda a\cos(\omega u)}-1$ and at $u=0$ equals $\sqrt{1+\lambda a}-1$. For $\delta=|\delta|(e_1+e_2)/\sqrt2$, again $\delta^3=0$ and $a(s,q)=(h_{11}+2h_{12}+h_{22})/(2)=A_\times(u)=b\sin(\omega u)$, so its strain is $\sqrt{1+\lambda b\sin(\omega u)}-1$, which is $0$ at $u=0$. This proves clause 3.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart ([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]]), let $(n,s)$
be an observer and propagation direction and let $p$, $h$, $\Sigma(n,s)$,
$\Pi_{n,s}$ and the amplitude terminology be as in
[[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]]. Write $V:=\mathbb R^4$ and let
$\mathcal S$ be the space of symmetric covariant $2$-tensors on $V$. Then:

**(a) Projections.** $p$ and $h$ are linear endomorphisms of $V$ with
$p^2=p$, $h^2=h$, $\ker p=\operatorname{span}\{n,s\}$,
$\operatorname{im}p=\Sigma(n,s)$, $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$,
$\operatorname{im}h=n^\perp$; both are $\eta$-self-adjoint,
$\eta(pu,v)=\eta(u,pv)$ and $\eta(hu,v)=\eta(u,hv)$ for all $u,v$. Moreover
$h-p=s^\flat\otimes s$, that is $h^a{}_b-p^a{}_b=s^as_b$.

**(b) Ranks and traces.** $\operatorname{rank}p=\dim\Sigma(n,s)=2$,
$p^a{}_a=2$, $\operatorname{rank}h=3$, $h^a{}_a=3$.

**(c) TT projection.** $\Pi_{n,s}$ is a linear endomorphism of $\mathcal S$
with $\Pi_{n,s}^2=\Pi_{n,s}$; for every $A\in\mathcal S$ the tensor
$\Pi_{n,s}(A)$ is TT with respect to $(n,s)$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]] clause (d); and $\Pi_{n,s}(A)=A$
exactly when $A$ is TT. The TT tensors form the two-dimensional linear
subspace $T_{n,s}=\{B\in\mathcal S:B(n,\cdot)=B(s,\cdot)=0,\ \eta^{ab}B_{ab}=0\}$,
so $\dim T_{n,s}=2$.

**(d) Orthogonal projection and amplitudes.** Let
$\langle A,B\rangle:=h^{ac}h^{bd}A_{ab}B_{cd}$ on the subspace of tensors
spatial with respect to $n$. This is a positive definite inner product, and
for every spatial $A$ and every TT $B$, $\langle A-\Pi_{n,s}(A),B\rangle=0$;
so $\Pi_{n,s}$ restricted to the spatial tensors is the orthogonal projection
onto $T_{n,s}$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]],
[[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]). With respect to an
ordered $\eta$-orthonormal screen basis $(e_1,e_2)$ a TT tensor is

$$B=B_{11}\bigl(e^1\otimes e^1-e^2\otimes e^2\bigr)+B_{12}\bigl(e^1\otimes e^2+e^2\otimes e^1\bigr),$$

so $B$ is determined by the pair $(A_+,A_\times)=(B_{11},B_{12})$, and under
a screen rotation by $\theta$ this pair transforms as in
[[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]] clause (c); in particular the map
$T_{n,s}\to\mathbb R^2$, $B\mapsto(A_+,A_\times)$, is a linear isomorphism.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ and metric components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Since the chart identifies each
$T_p\mathbb R^4$ with $\mathbb R^4$, all objects below are defined by their
components in this chart; they are the components at a point, and a subscript
$p$ is suppressed. Indices are raised and lowered with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]), and orthogonality is in
the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]].

**(a) Observer, propagation direction, screen.** Let $n=n^a\partial_a$ be an
**observer** of the flat model: $n$ is future-directed, $\eta(n,n)=-1$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); and let
$s=s^a\partial_a$ be a **propagation direction**: $\eta(s,s)=1$ and
$\eta(n,s)=0$. The pair defines the two-dimensional **screen**
$\Sigma(n,s):=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:\eta(v,n)=0,\ \eta(v,s)=0\}$, on which the
restriction of $\eta$ is positive definite by
[[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The **screen projector** and
the **spatial projector** of the pair are the $(1,1)$-tensors with components

$$p^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b-s^as_b,\qquad h^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b,$$

and the covariant form of the screen projector is
$p_{ab}:=\eta_{ac}p^c{}_b=\eta_{ab}+n_an_b-s_as_b$. The properties $p^2=p$,
$h^2=h$, $\operatorname{im}p=\Sigma(n,s)$ and $\operatorname{im}h=n^\perp$
are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page.

**(b) TT projection.** Let $A=(A_{ab})$ be a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
at a point. Its **transverse-traceless (TT) projection with respect to
$(n,s)$** is the symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$\Pi_{n,s}(A)_{ab}:=p_a{}^cp_b{}^dA_{cd}-\tfrac12\,p_{ab}\,p^{cd}A_{cd},\qquad p^{cd}:=\eta^{ce}\eta^{df}p_{ef}.$$

**(c) Screen amplitudes.** Let $(e_1,e_2)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $\Sigma(n,s)$ (which exists by
[[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]] applied
to the positive-definite restriction of $\eta$). For a symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor $A$ the **plus and cross amplitudes of $A$ with respect to
$(e_1,e_2)$** are $A_+:=A(e_1,e_1)$ and $A_\times:=A(e_1,e_2)$; if $A$ is
TT with respect to $(n,s)$ in the sense of clause (d) below, then in the dual
basis $(e^1,e^2)$ of the screen

$$A=A_+\bigl(e^1\otimes e^1-e^2\otimes e^2\bigr)+A_\times\bigl(e^1\otimes e^2+e^2\otimes e^1\bigr).$$

For a TT screen tensor $A$, under the rotation
$e_1'=\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2$,
$e_2'=-\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2$ of the screen basis the amplitudes
transform as $A_+'=A_+\cos2\theta+A_\times\sin2\theta$ and
$A_\times'=-A_+\sin2\theta+A_\times\cos2\theta$. Here $\sin$ and $\cos$
are the power-series functions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]];
expanding $A(e_1',e_1')$ and $A(e_1',e_2')$ by bilinearity and applying the
addition formulas of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] gives the two
displayed transformations.

**(d) TT tensors and TT perturbations.** A symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
$A$ is **transverse-traceless (TT) with respect to $(n,s)$** when
$A(n,\cdot)=0$, $A(s,\cdot)=0$ and $\eta^{ab}A_{ab}=0$. For a symmetric
field $h$ on an open set of the flat model, "TT with respect to $(n,s)$"
means that these three conditions hold at every point. A symmetric field $h$
is **spatial with respect to $n$** when $h(n,\cdot)=0$ at every point.

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the screen, the two projections and the
amplitude terminology, and states the rotation law of clause (c) as part of
the naming. It asserts no property of $\Pi_{n,s}$ (idempotence, rank, image
and trace are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page), no relation
to the planar perturbations of the plane-wave definition of this page
(established in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page) and no physical
interpretation of the amplitudes.

$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

derivations.claim: (Screen projection and trace.) In the adapted basis, $p^a{}_b=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1,0)$, so $p_a{}^cp_b{}^dA_{cd}$ keeps exactly the $11,12,21,22$ entries of $A$, namely $3,1,1,-1$, and kills the $13,23,33$ entries; the trace over the screen is $p^{cd}A_{cd}=A_{11}+A_{22}=3+(-1)=2$. This is clause 1.

(TT projection.) By [L1] and step 1.1, $(\Pi_{n,s}A)_{11}=\tfrac12(3-(-1))=2$, $(\Pi_{n,s}A)_{22}=-2$, $(\Pi_{n,s}A)_{12}=(\Pi_{n,s}A)_{21}=1$, all other components zero, which is the displayed matrix. Its contraction with $s=\partial_3$ vanishes because the $3$-row and $3$-column are zero; its trace is $\eta^{ab}(\Pi_{n,s}A)_{ab}=2+(-2)=0$; and applying the same rule to $\Pi_{n,s}(A)$, whose nonvanishing entries satisfy $2=-(-2)$ and $1=1$, returns the same matrix, so $\Pi_{n,s}^2(A)=\Pi_{n,s}(A)$. Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart and let $k\ne0$ be a null covector of the flat metric
([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]]). Let $\mathcal X$ be the real vector
space of symmetric $4\times4$ matrices (amplitudes), with trace
$\operatorname{tr}X=\eta^{ab}X_{ab}$ and trace reversal
$\bar X_{ab}=X_{ab}-\tfrac12\eta_{ab}\operatorname{tr}X$. Define the three
linear subspaces

$$V_0:=\{X\in\mathcal X:k^a\bar X_{ab}=0\ \text{for }b=0,1,2,3\},\qquad G:=\{X\in\mathcal X:X_{ab}=k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a\ \text{for some }Z\in\mathbb R^4\},$$

and, for an observer $n$ and propagation direction $s$ with
$k=\omega\,(\eta(n,\cdot)+\eta(s,\cdot))$, $\omega\ne0$, the space

$$T:=T_{n,s}=\{X\in\mathcal X:X(n,\cdot)=0,\ X(s,\cdot)=0,\ \operatorname{tr}X=0\}$$

of transverse-traceless amplitudes of
[[def-gr-wave-screen-and-tt-projection]] clause (d). Then:

**(a) Adapted frames exist.** There is a future-directed unit timelike $n$
with $\eta(n,k)\neq0$; putting $\omega:=-\eta(n,k)$ and
$s:=\eta^{-1}(k)/\omega-n$ (with $\eta^{-1}(k)$ the vector metrically dual
to $k$) gives $\eta(s,s)=1$, $\eta(n,s)=0$ and
$k=\omega(\eta(n,\cdot)+\eta(s,\cdot))$, and $(n,s)$ extends to an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^4$ with
$e_0=n$, $e_3=s$. In frame components
$k_A=k(e_A)=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ and $k^A=\omega(1,0,0,1)$.

**(b) The two subspaces lie in $V_0$ and meet trivially.** $G\subseteq V_0$
and $T\subseteq V_0$; the map $\mathbb R^4\to G$,
$Z\mapsto(k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a)$, is a linear isomorphism, so $\dim G=4$;
$\dim T=2$; and $T\cap G=\{0\}$. Consequently $\dim V_0=6$ and
$V_0=T\oplus G$.

**(c) Unique TT representative.** For every $X\in V_0$ there is exactly one
$Z\in\mathbb R^4$ such that $X'_{ab}:=X_{ab}-k_aZ_b-k_bZ_a$ is TT; in the
frame of (a) with $X_{AB}$ the frame components of $X$, the solution is

$$Z_0=-\frac{X_{00}}{2\omega},\qquad Z_1=-\frac{X_{01}}{\omega},\qquad Z_2=-\frac{X_{02}}{\omega},\qquad Z_3=Z_0-\frac{X_{03}}{\omega}.$$

Moreover the map $\pi:V_0\to T$, $\pi(X):=X'$, is linear and satisfies
$\pi|_{T}=\operatorname{id}_T$, so the quotient $V_0/G$ is isomorphic to
$T$; with a screen basis of $T$ as in [[lem-gr-tt-screen-projector]] clause
(d), the pair $(A_+,A_\times)=(X'_{11},X'_{12})$ is a linear isomorphism
$V_0/G\to\mathbb R^2$.

**(d) Differential form of the gauge condition and the gauge
transformation.** For a single-frequency plane wave $h_{ab}=X_{ab}\cos(k\cdot x)$
with amplitude $X\in\mathcal X$, the harmonic-gauge condition
$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0$ of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause
(d) holds exactly when $X\in V_0$. If $X\in V_0$ and $Z$ is as in (c), the
covector field $\xi_b:=Z_b\sin(k\cdot x)$ satisfies
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a=(k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a)\cos(k\cdot x)$, so that
$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ is the plane wave with
amplitude $X'$ and is again in harmonic gauge.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ and constant metric components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$
be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under the chart; all
components and all partial derivatives below are taken in this chart. Let
$c>0$ be a real parameter. Throughout, a **symmetric field** means a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $\Omega$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) and indices are raised and
lowered with $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{-1}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]).

**(a) Phase coordinate and wave covector.** The **phase coordinate** of the
planar waves of this page is $u(x):=x^0-x^3$. Its differential $n:=du$ has
components $n_a=\delta^0_a-\delta^3_a$, so that $n_0=1$, $n_3=-1$,
$n_1=n_2=0$ and $\eta^{ab}n_an_b=-1+1=0$: $n$ is a nonzero null covector, and
the vector with spatial components $(0,0,-1)$ has Euclidean norm $1$ in the
sense of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The vector $T:=\partial_0+\partial_3$
is null and future-directed, and $\eta(T,\cdot)=-n$, so that the phase
covector is the metric dual of $-T$. For $\omega\in\mathbb R$ we call
$k_a:=\omega\,\eta_{ab}T^b=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ a **wave covector**; $\omega$
is its real phase coefficient and $|\omega|$ its absolute value. Its raised components are $k^a=\omega T^a=
\omega(1,0,0,1)$, so that $k\ne0$ for $\omega\ne0$ and $k^ak_a=0$. For a
general null covector $k\ne0$ of the flat model the adapted orthonormal
frames are treated in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page; clauses
(a)-(d) fix the standard propagation direction $x^3$ used on this page.

**(b) Planar perturbations and TT profiles.** A symmetric field $h$ on
$\Omega$ is a **planar perturbation** when there is a smooth map
$F=(F_{ab}):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{4\times4}$ with values in the symmetric
matrices such that $h_{ab}(x)=F_{ab}(u(x))$ for all $x\in\Omega$; such an
$F$ is a **planar profile**. The image $u(\Omega)$ is open: near each
$x\in\Omega$, varying $x^0$ through a sufficiently small interval varies
$u(x)$ through an interval while remaining in $\Omega$. The restriction
$F|_{u(\Omega)}$ is uniquely determined by $h$, but an extension of it outside
$u(\Omega)$ is not determined unless $u(\Omega)=\mathbb R$. A planar
perturbation is **transverse traceless (TT) with respect to the inertial
frame** when $h_{a0}=h_{a3}=0$ and $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$;
equivalently, a chosen profile satisfies $F_{a0}=F_{a3}=0$ and
$F_{11}+F_{22}=0$ on $u(\Omega)$. In that case its restriction to
$u(\Omega)$ has the form

$$F_{ab}(u)=A_+(u)\bigl(\delta^1_a\delta^1_b-\delta^2_a\delta^2_b\bigr)+A_\times(u)\bigl(\delta^1_a\delta^2_b+\delta^2_a\delta^1_b\bigr)$$

for smooth functions $A_+,A_\times:u(\Omega)\to\mathbb R$, uniquely given by
$A_+=F_{11}|_{u(\Omega)}$ and $A_\times=F_{12}|_{u(\Omega)}$; these are the
**plus and cross amplitudes** on the phase image. In particular a TT planar perturbation is
spatial ($h_{a0}=0$), traceless ($\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=0$) and transverse (its
contraction with the wave covector of (a) vanishes).

**(c) Single-frequency plane waves.** Let $k\ne0$ be a null covector of the
flat model and let $X=(X_{ab})$ and $Y=(Y_{ab})$ be real symmetric matrices.
The symmetric field

$$h_{ab}(x):=X_{ab}\cos(k\cdot x)+Y_{ab}\sin(k\cdot x),\qquad k\cdot x:=k_ax^a,$$

where $\cos$ and $\sin$ are the power-series functions
([[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]), is the **plane-wave perturbation
with wave covector $k$ and amplitudes $(X,Y)$**. Its **trace-reversed
amplitudes** are $\bar X_{ab}:=X_{ab}-\tfrac12\eta_{ab}\eta^{cd}X_{cd}$ and
$\bar Y_{ab}:=Y_{ab}-\tfrac12\eta_{ab}\eta^{cd}Y_{cd}$, in agreement with the
trace reversal of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (c). The
plane wave is **in harmonic gauge** when $k^a\bar X_{ab}=0$ and
$k^a\bar Y_{ab}=0$. The plane wave is **TT with respect to the wave covector
$k$** when, in some $\eta$-orthonormal frame $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0$
future timelike, $e_1,e_2$ spanning the screen of (d) and
$k_A=k(e_A)=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ for some $\omega\ne0$ (existence of such a
frame is proved in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page, where also
$k^A=\omega(1,0,0,1)$), both amplitude matrices have components
$X_{a0}=X_{a3}=Y_{a0}=Y_{a3}=0$ and $X_{11}+X_{22}=Y_{11}+Y_{22}=0$ in that
frame.

**(d) Screen amplitudes.** In the situation of (c) with
$k_A=\omega(-1,0,0,1)$ in the adapted frame, the **screen** of $k$ is the two-dimensional linear
subspace $\Sigma_k:=\{v\in T_p\mathbb R^4:\eta(v,e_0)=\eta(v,e_3)=0\}$,
which is independent of the point $p$ and is the orthogonal complement of
$\operatorname{span}\{e_0,e_3\}$ in the sense of
[[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **plus and cross
amplitudes of a screen tensor** $A$ (a symmetric bilinear form on
$\Sigma_k$) with respect to an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2)$
of $\Sigma_k$ are $A_+:=A(e_1,e_1)$ and $A_\times:=A(e_1,e_2)$.

**(e) Linearized field equations.** Let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a real
parameter and let $S=(S_{ab})$ be a symmetric field on $\Omega$. A symmetric
field $h$ **solves the linearized field equation with source $S$ and
parameter $\Lambda$** when $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)+\Lambda h_{ab}=S_{ab}$ on
$\Omega$, with $G^{(1)}$ the first-order Einstein coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (b). It **solves the
linearized vacuum equations** when $S=0$ and $\Lambda=0$; and it **solves the
linearized vacuum equations with parameter $\Lambda$** when $S=0$ and
$\Lambda$ is arbitrary. A planar perturbation (b) or a plane wave (c) is a
**linearized vacuum wave** when it solves the linearized vacuum equations
with $\Lambda=0$.

**(f) Scope.** This item fixes objects and terminology only. It asserts no
existence of a profile or amplitude solving any equation, no relation between
the single-frequency and planar descriptions, and no physical
interpretation; in particular the harmonic-gauge condition in (c) is a named
algebraic condition whose equivalence with the differential condition of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (d) is proved in the
gauge-decomposition lemma of this page, and the terminology "TT" in (b)-(c)
is defined relative to a chosen orthonormal frame and not claimed to be
geometrically canonical.

derivations.claim: (Membership in $V_0$ and failure of TT.) The trace is $\operatorname{tr}X=\eta^{ab}X_{ab}=-X_{00}+X_{11}+X_{22}+X_{33}=2+1-1+2=4$, so $\bar X_{ab}=X_{ab}-2\eta_{ab}$ has entries $\bar X_{00}=-2+2=0$, $\bar X_{01}=-2$, $\bar X_{03}=0$, $\bar X_{11}=1-2=-1$, $\bar X_{13}=2$, $\bar X_{22}=-1-2=-3$, $\bar X_{33}=2-2=0$ and $\bar X_{12}=\bar X_{23}=0$. With $k^0=1$, $k^3=1$, $k^1=k^2=0$, the four contractions are $k^a\bar X_{a0}=\bar X_{00}+\bar X_{30}=0$, $k^a\bar X_{a1}=\bar X_{01}+\bar X_{31}=-2+2=0$, $k^a\bar X_{a2}=0$, $k^a\bar X_{a3}=\bar X_{03}+\bar X_{33}=0$; hence $X\in V_0$. It is not TT because $X(e_0,e_0)=X_{00}=-2\ne0$ and $\operatorname{tr}X=4\ne0$. This is clause 1.

(The TT representative.) By [L1] with $\omega=1$ the unique $Z$ is $Z_0=-X_{00}/2=1$, $Z_1=-X_{01}=2$, $Z_2=-X_{02}=0$, $Z_3=Z_0-X_{03}=1$, which is the displayed $Z$. Forming $k_aZ_b+k_bZ_a$ with $k_a=(-1,0,0,1)$ gives the matrix with entries $(kZ+Zk)_{00}=-2$, $(kZ+Zk)_{01}=-2$, $(kZ+Zk)_{03}=0$, $(kZ+Zk)_{11}=0$, $(kZ+Zk)_{13}=2$, $(kZ+Zk)_{22}=0$, $(kZ+Zk)_{23}=0$, $(kZ+Zk)_{33}=2$, and subtracting from $X$ gives the displayed $X'$, whose only nonzero entries are $X'_{11}=1$ and $X'_{22}=-1$; hence $A_+=X'_{11}=1$ and $A_\times=X'_{12}=0$. This is clause 2.

(The perturbation.) By [L2] the gauge-transformed perturbation of the plane wave $h_{ab}=X_{ab}\cos(k\cdot x)$ is $h'=X'\cos(k\cdot x)$, and $X'\in T\subseteq V_0$ is TT and in harmonic gauge in the sense of [[def-gr-plane-wave-perturbation]] clause (c). This is clause 3.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $\Omega\subseteq M$ be an open set of the flat model
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]], let
$(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over $\Omega$ with
first-order coefficients $\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}$, $S^{(1)}$, $G^{(1)}_{ab}$ and with trace
reversal $\bar h$, d'Alembertian $\Box$ and gauge transformation
$h'_{ab}=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ as in
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]], and let $L>0$ be a length scale.
All components are taken in the inertial chart and all contractions are
with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$.

**(a) Christoffel symbols.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
constant $C_K<\infty$ such that for all $p\in K$ and
$0<|\lambda|\le\varepsilon_1/2$,

$$\Bigl|\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,\eta^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bh_{cd}+\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_dh_{bc}\bigr).$$

**(b) Ricci tensor.** With the same constants (enlarged if necessary),

$$\Bigl|\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_c\partial_a h^{c}{}_{b}+\partial_c\partial_b h^{c}{}_{a}-\Box h_{ab}-\partial_a\partial_b h\bigr).$$

**(c) Scalar curvature and Einstein tensor.** With the same constants,

$$\Bigl|S(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,S^{(1)}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad S^{(1)}=\partial_a\partial_bh^{ab}-\Box h,$$

and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\lambda,p)-\lambda\,G^{(1)}_{ab}(p)\Bigr|\le C_K\,\lambda^2,\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h_{ab}+\partial^c\partial_{(a}\bar h_{b)c}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\partial^d\bar h_{cd}.$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on
$\Omega$,

$$\bar h'{}_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a+\eta_{ab}\,\partial^c\xi_c,\qquad \partial^a\bar h'{}_{ab}=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}-\Box\xi_b .$$

Consequently $h'$ is in harmonic gauge exactly when
$\Box\xi_b=\partial^a\bar h_{ab}$, and in that case

$$G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=-\tfrac12\,\Box\bar h'{}_{ab}.$$

**(e) Gauge invariance of the first-order curvature.** For every smooth
covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}(h),\qquad S^{(1)}(h')=S^{(1)}(h),\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}(h')=G^{(1)}_{ab}(h).$$

That is, subtracting the pure-gauge perturbation
$\partial_a\xi_b+\partial_b\xi_a$ from the first-order perturbation leaves
the first-order Ricci, scalar and Einstein tensors unchanged; their
first-order coefficients depend on $h$ only through its gauge-equivalence
class.

**(f) Quadratic remainder.** For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ there are
$\delta_0>0$ and $C_K<\infty$ such that for every smooth symmetric component
field $A=(A_{ab})$ on a neighborhood of $K$ with

$$B_K(A):=\sup_K\max_{a,b}|A_{ab}|+L\sup_K\max_{a,b,c}|\partial_cA_{ab}|+L^2\sup_K\max_{a,b,c,d}|\partial_c\partial_dA_{ab}|\le\delta_0,$$

the metric $\eta+A$ is Lorentzian of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $K$ and

$$\Bigl|G_{ab}(\eta+A)(p)-G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)(p)\Bigr|\le \frac{C_K\,B_K(A)^2}{L^2}\qquad(p\in K),$$

where $G^{(1)}_{ab}(A)$ is the right-hand side of the displayed formula of
(c) with $h$ replaced by $A$, and $G_{ab}(\eta+A)$ is the Einstein tensor of
the metric with components $\eta_{ab}+A_{ab}$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

derivations.claim: (Trace, harmonic gauge and admissibility.) The trace is $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}=h_{11}+h_{22}=\cos U-\cos U=0$, so $\bar h=h$. The divergence components are $\partial^ah_{a0}=0$; for $b=1$, $\partial^ah_{a1}=\eta^{00}\partial_0h_{01}+\eta^{11}\partial_1h_{11}+\eta^{33}\partial_3h_{31}=0+0+0=0$, since $h$ does not depend on $x^1$ and $h_{31}=0$; similarly for $b=2,3$. Hence $\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0$: the perturbation is in harmonic gauge. Also, [L3] gives $g_{11}=1+\lambda\cos U>0$ and $g_{22}=1-\lambda\cos U>0$ for $|\lambda|<\tfrac12$, with $g_{00}=-1$ and $g_{33}=1$, so $g(\lambda)$ is Lorentzian and $h$ is an admissible first-order perturbation.

(The flat d'Alembertian of the profile.) By [L2]-[L3], $\Box f(U)=(-v^2+1)f''(U)=\tfrac34(-\cos U)=-\tfrac34\cos U$. Hence $\Box h_{11}=-\tfrac34\cos U$, $\Box h_{22}=\tfrac34\cos U$ and $\Box h_{ab}=0$ for all other pairs.

(The linearized Einstein tensor.) By [L1] and steps 1.1-1.2, $G^{(1)}_{11}(h)=-\tfrac12\Box\bar h_{11}=\tfrac38\cos U$, which equals $\tfrac38$ wherever $U=0$. Therefore $G^{(1)}_{ab}(h)$ is not identically zero and the perturbation does not solve the linearized vacuum equations on $\mathbb R^4$, refuting the statement.
